speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Without wanting to engage in debate, I would ask that the Member, if he is going to state policy of another Party, do it correctly. Our policy is that the issue is between the woman and her doctor. They are the ones who will decide.

Once again, I have riled up the New Democrats. Why is the Hon. Member's Leader deciding what

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
the Tory Government thinks about families? The Member should stick to the subject. This New Democratic Party has no handle or exclusivity on who represents Canadians and families.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext: Ask your spouse.
Even the Liberals have to admit that this was a very bold policy that our Minister brought forward-

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext: They wouldn't lie as much.

The Liberals are prepared to accept it. I am sure many of the New Democrats, when they get out on the hustings, will be told not to throw money away recklessly. They are going to be asked to put a price tag on what they propose to do and will be told to make sure the money is used in a very effective and efficient way. Obviously Canadians are not prepared to give that Party an opportunity to start spending Canadian dollars. Never will they do that.
When their Leader announced this great day care policy, I believe a couple of weeks ago, I did not read any editorials about how great it was. The policy seems to have finally died. It will be comical during the next federal election to know where the New Democrats will get all the money for their day care promises and all the things they have proposed. They have not figured how to keep people working or how to create more jobs. They will just borrow money like the former Government did.
Canadians will never give the New Democrats the opportunity to implement some of these wild, woolly, witchy, wacky ideas which they scheme up, I guess in their caucus rooms, and whoever else schemes them up. Their policies are not sound and they probably never will be sound. Their Leader basically condemned most of the women in this country for staying home to look after their own children, saying that all they do is watch TV and that is not day care. That is the New Democratic Party policy of the way they think of women in this country. A mother does not look after her own child well enough. She is considered a poor person in the provision of quality day care. That is the attitude of New Democrats. They are going to get somebody else to do it.
The Government will spend the money and provide this new, wonderful, quality day care. Probably New Democrats are not capable of looking after their own children. They need a lot of assistance. They cannot do it on their own. They need help from the Government. They need some expert to tell them how to change diapers and what their children should eat. That is what the New Democrats want.
I think we know now where New Democrats stand. We know their game. It is just fuddle-duddle promises and that is all it will end up being.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to the child care program the Government says it is putting in place. I find it rather sad that from a Government that is supposed to be trying to put a new face on its activities and to keep its promises, we have a Bill that is full of puffery. It is window-dressing and trickery with figures. It will not meet our present needs, and it puts a cap on the natural growth that was already in place.
Under the Canada Assistance Plan, without this new program, the federal Government would have spent, assuming an inflationary factor of only 5 per cent a year, $17 billion over the next seven years. The total federal spending over that same period of time could now be slightly more than $22 billion or 4 per cent per year more than we now have without this new program.
On top of all that, there is a catch. We do not know if even one nickel will be spent in each of the provinces. It takes a federal-provincial agreement with each province to put this into place. As Marjorie Nichols points out, we have to use a conditional tense when talking about child care anywhere within Canada. Certainly we will not have a national child care system with national standards and objectives which must be met.
We talk about the low birth rate in Canada. We talk about our concern for the family and the family structure. We talk about children as being our future. One of the most important building blocks in our society is the child care system, whether it is for pre-school children or for school children with two working parents, children called latchkey children.
I become dreadfully sad when I recall going before the royal commission on the status of women, chaired by Senator Florence Bird. We brought the concern over latch key children into the public view, and we discussed how important it was to ensure that these children had good supervision after school hours so that their parents could work with free minds. Their parents needed two salaries to make ends meet. At that time, we were talking about the working poor but now we are talking about all families. The traditional family with the mother staying home is only one out of every ten families. We are not facing the reality of the society in which we live.
We will not end up with a national program; we will end up with 10 separate agreements with 10 different standards. According to the Meech Lake Accord, we were supposed to have national objectives. This new look at the Constitution would provide for good cost-shared programs with the thought that across Canada there would be equivalent programs. There is no dazzling multi-billion program for day care across this land.
The spending increases will be absolutely minimal. In fact, they are paltry, to use the word of Marjorie Nichols. About $570,000 a year would be made available beyond what is already available under the Canada Assistance Plan. Further, the provinces that want to enter into the national day care
August 23, 1988

program have to opt out of the Canada Assistance Plan. A cap has been put on the growth of this very key sector in society.
I believe that when Conservatives are out on the hustings and have to face the electorate, they will be very embarrassed by the fact that no one will be tricked into thinking that saying that they have put in a great national child care system means that they have really done so, because they have not. In reality, this let's pretend child care program is supposed to provide $6.4 billion over seven years, but $2.3 billion of that total is in the form of new tax deductions on credits announced in the February Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). I am not against that, but those are certainly not new dollars for new child care spaces.
The child care legislation we are addressing today contains exactly $4 billion. However, we have forgotten that $1.9 billion of that $4 billion is already being spent annually by the federal Government through the Canada Assistance Plan on child care items. We have in reality a provision for $2.6 billion in new federal funds for direct spending, from which the $1.9 billion that is already being spent annually is subtracted, ending up with that marvellous amount of $560,000 a year being made available for new programs. That new money will certainly be sufficient for the much needed 200,000 spaces, but that will not answer the needs of another one million children who need this service.
Our Party feels that parents should have the right to choose, but they should also have the right to choose child care services that will be of quality, that will be affordable, and that will have standards for the teachers who will be paid commensurately as they provide the loving care that is needed for young children, and they should have programs in which they will have a say. None of those things have been articulated in this Bill, and I regret the sleight of hand, the use of language which is not reflected in reality in this Bill.
The unvarnished facts are embarrassing to the Government. I hope that each and every government Member will feel the discomfort as their constituents ask them about this not-national, not-good, poorly-conceived child care plan which they think will help the development of Canada and its future. I would suggest that when this Bill goes into legislative committee, government Members carefully consider the kinds of amendments that will truly reflect the needs of our children and their futures in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate having the opportunity to say a few words on the child care Bill, Bill C-144. I will take my allotted time to speak particularly about rural Canada.
This time of year in rural Canada should be time of rejoicing and abundance while in the process of harvesting the crops. Right now, however, the farm community is not a happy community, and there are good reasons for this.
For the last five or six years, the impact of the economy has been building up to the point where farm communities are in a
Canada Child Care Act
very bad state. Prices have risen considerably in the last little while, but that is not having the impact it should on the farm community.
Rural Canada is made up of something over 200,000 farms and the villages and towns with their schools, churches, and medical facilities which serve those farms. For the last several years an average of eight farmers per day have been leaving the farm for reasons such as bankruptcy, foreclosure, and so on. That has not slowed down. In fact, the number is increasing each year. Consequently, farming communities are becoming more isolated. It is because of this situation that farming has become one of the most stressful occupations in the country. The farm suicide rate has tripled since 1981 and now stands at double the national average. There are many cases of rural family violence, much more than we ever thought would happen on the farm.
The bulk of farmers having financial problems are those between the ages of 30 and 45 years. They are highly productive farmers who have committed themselves to farming and they produce a great deal, but they are unable to keep up. It is those same families who have young children that need care.
Those farmers who are staying on the farm and those people in the small communities surrounding the farms are the people we are concerned about right now. A lot of the people leaving their farms are just moving into the surrounding towns or the nearest city. However, a lot of them are attempting to hang on, and they are the ones we need to talk about specifically.
There are probably three categories that we can point to of people who are attempting to stay on the farm and need some assistance with child care. There is the family where one or two members go to the nearest town or city to work. At the same time they attempt to keep the farm going.
There are farm families who move to the city so that the man, in most cases, can drive out to the farm and keep it going. There is a third group which has to be recognized as well. This group stays on the farm but attempts to eliminate all outside help. They try to keep the farm going with the family alone. Every member of the family has to take some responsibility for keeping the farm going.
Right now some farm men and women, in fact perhaps more women than men, are actually doing three jobs at the same time. They are working at a store or office in town, teaching school or driving a school bus to bring in some cash. They also take a certain amount of responsibility to keep the farm going. They do regular farm work and assist in keeping it going. They also take care of the children, raise the family.
Right now child care is a very unpopular concept in rural Canada because there is nothing in this Bill that indicates that rural Canada will be taken care of. There is nothing to indicate that they will have child care in those areas. As one lady told me yesterday, this is another federal program which we in

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
rural Canada will not be able to access. In most cases this involves small towns and villages of 50 to 75 people.
That is one of the things wrong with this approach to child care. We need to look at the specific requirements of rural Canada and make sure that either child care spaces or other arrangements can be made to make sure that the family is able to stay together and keep the farm going.
The federal Government spends huge amounts of money on things which are far less important to Canada than the raising of a family. We should not hesitate to pay people to assist the parents in raising their children. Doing that is a good investment for Canada. We should do it in such a way that it reaches out to those areas and those people who need it most.
Right now many people in rural Canada need assistance in raising their families. They need child care. Consequently, we should provide the spaces or provide the people or the money so that they are able to do a good job of raising a family. This Bill does not indicate to the rural community that any real care has been taken with respect to child care in rural Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate on this legislation, the Canada Child Care Act. I believe it is an initiative which will enable our Government to implement a major part of our new national child care strategy, which includes not only the provisions of this Act but the creation of 200,000 additional child care spaces. As well, there is the tax assistance to families which will be of great benefit to many men and women across this country, and the child initiatives fund.
It is interesting to look at the whole issue of child care and who should be responsible. I am pleased to see a change in attitude across the country on this issue. Recently the Vancouver Board of Trade, the largest business organization in Vancouver, issued a copy of its report making a case for quality child care services in British Columbia. It notes in its report that by the year 2000, 80 per cent of all new workforce members will be women, minorities, or immigrants, and that one-half of all women employees will have babies while they are employed. These facts translate into a need for employers of all types and sizes to deal with child care issues for their own self-interest. In fact, the Board of Trade quotes from some studies done by Fortune Magazine which report that 41 per cent of parents surveyed lost at least one day's work in the three months prior to the poll in order to care for sick children, and nearly 10 per cent took three to five days off for such purposes. Child care problems were also a major cause of unproductive time at work or the production of lower than normal quality work. Obviously, by addressing the child care issue, businesses can achieve greater stability and productivity in their workforces.
It is very interesting to note that the Vancouver Board of Trade goes on in its brief to suggest certain initiatives that the
provincial Government should take to respond to our new federal child care strategy and it went on to outline what it believes employers should be doing. The whole issue of child care is a relationship of four parts: the family, the parents, the employer, and the federal and provincial Governments. Each has a role to play in order for us to address the situation.
I am pleased that the legislation before us provides for the implementation of the goal which was announced last December, "an additional 200,000 new subsidized spaces which will require a federal commitment of some $3 billion". However, on the basis of the plans submitted by the provincial Governments over the last six months, it has become clear that additional financial assistance would be required if we were to meet the goal of 200,000 spaces, as well as ensure the quality of the system as a whole and that the existing spaces continue to improve.
We are aware that just last month the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) announced on behalf of the Government that we were committing an additional $1 billion to the child care program. We are not prepared to sacrifice quality for quantity. Both are equally important to parents whose children will be utilizing the child care system.
Just to share some information about how this new system will work, during the next seven years, which we are calling the "boost period", we intend to support the creation of 200,000 additional subsidized child care spaces. In effect, this will double the size of the current subsidized system. It has taken about 15 years for us to reach the level of 200,000 spaces and in seven years we will double that.
To assist the provinces, because delivery of the services is a provincial responsibility, we will provide 75 per cent of the capital costs involved in the development of new spaces in nonprofit child care agencies during the seven year period. As well, we will provide for 50 per cent of ongoing operating costs for both non-profit and commercial agencies. There have been a lot of questions of why "both", and certain groups have said only non-profit agencies should be eligible for the subsidies. However, we made the decision to include commercial agencies under the terms of the legislation. We recognize that we cannot ignore the basic fact that a full 40 per cent of subsidized child care spaces now being provided are being provided by the commercial sector. The reason our national policy on child care is a workable policy is that it builds upon a system that currently exists and adapts to the regional diversity of this country.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, from my involvement with child care, there is obviously some agencies that are better than others, but I have found excellent child care facilities operating in the commercial sector and excellent facilities working in the non-profit area. I do not believe that either side should be penalized, and I am pleased to see we have included both in our strategy.
This legislation will also permit the Government to increase
the rate of cost sharing for certain provinces based upon a
August 23, 1988

national average entitlement per child formula. We have included this special provision to assist parents and children who reside in provinces which are attempting to catch up to other parts of Canada in what they spend on child care. This is a national strategy. We believe that child care facilities and services should be more available in all parts of the country.
1 might point out that Clause 4 of the legislation sets out the various terms and conditions which will form part of a negotiated agreement between the federal Government and each province. These will include the annual federal commitment to the province, the number of spaces to be created during the seven-year period, and the basis for subsequent cost sharing agreements with respect to child care services.
I wanted to respond as well to some comments made earlier by the Eton. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) who indicated that the current provisions under the Canada Assistance Plan would have resulted in $3 billion a year being spent on child care services. She is wrong. That is not the reality. The reality is that at the moment, between the federal and provincial Governments, we are spending about $480 million of which $160 million is federal money. Therefore, the provinces are spending $320 million a year. There is no way the provinces are going to be able to increase their expenditures, so they could theoretically take advantage of the maximum CAP funding. That is just not the real world.
In fact, the present CAP provisions do not include funding for the capital cost for the building or renovating, so there is no assistance there. There is no incentive for the creation of new spaces. Even in the operating area where it is 50 per cent of eligible costs, there are many costs which are not eligible. What actually occurs is that the federal Government ends up subsidizing only about 35 per cent of the total costs. The changes in the new child care strategy in the legislation we have before us, as I mentioned, are 75 per cent on capital cost and 50 per cent on operating and new criteria for establishing that 50 per cent. In the first year alone our contribution will double, and by the end of the seven years it is estimated that the federal contribution will be in the order of $800 million a year.
We will have spent, then, the estimated $4 billion for the creation of those spaces. This legislation is important to the women, to the parents, and to the children of this country. I would ask my colleagues on all sides of the House to give it early consideration so that the system can go into effect, the provinces can complete their negotiations, and those who are involved in establishing a child care agency and child care spaces can get on with the job of creating the spaces and the opportunities for families to have child care available to them.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to participate in this debate. I would like to preface my comments by thanking my Liberal colleagues who have allowed me to speak first so I can go home and spend some time with my daughter. We talk about Parliament and the opportunities for women being equal with men, but the reality
Canada Child Care Act
is that when we are having sitting sessions until ten o'clock every night, week upon week, to try to shove some government Bills through, that is simply not happening. That is just a practical note, Mr. Speaker.
I would also like to spend some time outlining what I consider the giant fraud being perpetrated on the people of Canada in the over-all area of child policy. Let us not forget that this so-called child care policy is coming from a Government that has done everything in its power to cut back the purchasing power of the ordinary family. It has cut back on the child tax deductions from about $370 to about $60 over the course of its time in office. It has cut back on family allowances. What we should really be seeing here tonight is an overall policy for children which really does permit parents to make real choices.
Government Members tried to deindex senior citizens' pensions and they were not successful, but they were successful in doing it with the family allowances because families with children are not necessarily the most powerful voices in our society.
I only have 10 minutes so I would like to focus on what I consider to be the glaring contradictions in this so-called national policy for children. When parents are put in a position, either by choice or by economic necessity, of working outside the home and having to put their child in care other than their own, they want to be sure their child is safe.
I think that is the paramount concern of every parent. That is why the Government must include some national standards in announcing a policy. Yet, it has failed miserably in doing so because the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) is introducing a Bill that permits the provinces to set whatever standards they want. There is no national level of care whereby parents in Corner Brook, Newfoundland, should have the same level of care for their child as a child in Toronto. That is not the case because there are no national standards.
According to the preamble of the Bill, the Government caps the amount of spending. Rather than indicate that the program will expand, it is putting a lid on it.
The previous Liberal Government established a program of subsidized child care spaces that was geared toward low-income earners. There was no limit on that program. The Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) was wrong when she said that the only difference between the previous Liberal program, which was instituted at a time when we were not even sure about the so-called child care crisis, was spending an amount of about 4 per cent per year.
There are no national standards in the Tory child care plan. There are rather generous tax deductions. The tax deductions are being doubled from $2,000 to $4,000 a year per child. As a parent who is earning a salary that is significantly above the

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
national average, I stand to benefit much more directly from the Government's child tax deduction than a woman in my riding who is working at the Hamilton General Hospital and may be earning $6 an hour.
If I am in the 50 per cent tax bracket and I get a $4,000 tax deduction, that is money in my pocket. However, a woman who is earning $6 an hour and is paying only 15 per cent or 20 per cent in income tax, her benefit is cut by two-thirds. We believe that the tax deduction system is wrong and should be replaced by a tax credit system which would see direct payments to parents, but would start by giving the most money to those parents who are at the lowest end of the income scale.
When one considers the lack of national standards and the fact that the child tax deduction will benefit the rich, it provides a rather clear picture of what policy the Tories want to establish. It has no national objectives.
What have we seen from the New Democratic Party? Its Leader announced that he would like to cut child care spending by about 30 per cent. He wants to spend about 30 per cent less than the Conservative Government, and will do that by eliminating any direct payments to families. A steelworker in my riding who gets a $2,000 tax deduction would lose that under an NDP Government.
Under an NDP Government, the Liberal initiative of a tax credit which would be more beneficial to the low and middle income earners would also be gone. The NDP does not believe in the right of the individual to make choices for themselves. It believes that everything should be run by the Government in an institutionalized fashion.
Wrong, and you know it.

Let me speak from personal experience. I have a terrific child care giver in my neighbourhood in Ottawa. Her name is Clotilde Keklikian. She has just given birth to another child of her own and now has three children. I probably could not have found a better care giver than her under any circumstances. She happens to have voluntarily associated herself with a licensing service. She would meet the need for national standards, but because she receives payment in her home, according to the NDP definition she is part of the massive profit-making conspiracy that would, of necessity, not be allowed under their policy.
Is that making a profit?

I am very happy to hear the NDP defend its policy because I am rather shocked that it would introduce a situation in which a woman like Clotilde Keklikian would not be able to qualify under its system.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member knows full well that the NDP supports family home day care. The woman to whom she is referring sounds like an excellent care giver. There is no reason why she should not be licensed. In fact, she would have many advantages with
extra subsidies under our plan if she were licensed as a family day care giver.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the Hon. Member for Vancouver East will make a few comments on this matter later tonight. The Hon. Member for Hamilton East has the floor.

The NDP has not answered the basic question. Why is it cutting $3 billion from a child care program? There are parents who are currently spending thousands of dollars. Certainly it is very difficult for a steelworker in my riding to come up with the money that is necessary, yet under an NDP Government, that steelworker would probably see a reduction in his disposable income by some $1,000 to $3,000, depending on the number of children. The NDP is wiping out any direct tax credits or tax deductions to families. If that is the case, I would like the NDP to explain why its Leader said last week that he would be spending about one-third less of what is being spent under the Government's program.
There are some fundamental differences. The Liberal Party wants national standards. We also want tax credits as opposed to tax deductions. I have not heard the NDP speak out on this. According to the NDP definition, those who are in family care, who meet national standards and may be making a small profit, would be out of the picture. We believe that those people can also give good care.
Most important, the Liberal Party would introduce a child policy that supports all families and that offers women real opportunity and real choice, not simply a government program, which, over seven years, will result in a near 4 per cent annual increase in spending.
We want to see a program directed not only toward women and families who are working outside the home, but also toward women working in the home because we believe their contribution is just as valuable.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof.
I think we can conclude after what has been said so far, Mr. Speaker, that all three Parties agree on the substance of this Bill. We all agree that today, day-care is becoming an increasingly essential service. However, we do not agree on how funding should be allocated and made available to the public.
Mr. Speaker, I think that first of all, and this is very important, it is a matter of philosophy. I heard my colleague speak earlier about deductions and tax credits. We have opted for tax measures. Other political parties, groups and individuals who made their positions known across this country told us we should focus on establishing a national service paid for by
August 23, 1988

the State, to ensure the availability of such services and provide a number of guarantees. That is more or less the position taken by the NDP. However, in the first place, it is a matter of philosophy, a matter of how we look at the services to be offered to the customer and how we react to an increasingly pressing need.
Mr. Speaker, we can either provide the money or provide the opportunity to spend that money. We have opted for the former.
1 remember, and I think we have lived long enough with a Liberal Government to understand the Liberal approach, when we had an economic problem. The Government invented the Canada Works projects, so-called winter works, in the belief that by creating temporary jobs, it would be able to deal with economic problems, and so billions of dollars were spent every year. The Government spent enormous amounts of money on Canada Works projects which tended to come back every year, with a few new ones. That was one way of looking at the problem.
The Conservative Government and its Prime Minister, Brian Mulroney, decided to opt for another solution, more in line with the philosophy of the Conservative Party, which is a philosophy of free enterprise, a philosophy of supporting developers. It provides Canadian decision makers with the economic conditions that tend to attract investors. That is the big difference. Our opponents however, would set up a program and then they would decide to index it. .. all of a sudden they discovered indexation. That was a wonderful discovery. After sliced bread, indexation is just about the best thing ever invented in Canada. Indexing means that starting today, tomorrow will be like yesterday, but indexed, a little better than yesterday. We cannot build an economy that way! I have never bought clothes from a tailor by saying that I would pay last year's price, indexed. I never bought a car that way, but we have built an economy that way. My colleague was just talking about it. He talked about family allowance, old age security pensions, the MPs' pension fund. It covers everything!
But in my opinion, it is not the right way to develop the economy because it does not teach individuals how to fish-it gives them fish. If in one year they needed a certain amount and the next year the economy has grown by 3 per cent, automatically they are given a 3 per cent increase-that is indexation. We, for our part, give people the opportunity to choose. And in doing so, Mr. Speaker-our program was so popular, we wanted to add about 200,000 spaces and we will have to give out money; we have to give out more money because of the very positive response from the provinces.
We must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that child care is a provincial responsibility. And so on . . . We could not stick our nose in a field of provincial jurisdiction even if we wanted to. We can set up a national program that the provinces could join, that the federal Government could participate in and that would gradually bring people up to the national standards.
Canada Child Care Act
The Liberals suggest directly administering a program in a field of provincial jurisdiction. They are telling the provinces that they are incapable of running day care facilities, just as they are unable to read the Free Trade Agreement, so the Liberals would do all that for them. They tell the provinces not to worry, that they will decide for them and run the day care centres, even if it is a provincial responsibility, and they will force the provinces to accept national standards.
We too, Mr. Speaker, would like to have national standards of quality, and they are being developed, but this necessarily involves each of the ten Canadian provinces and each of the territories. This means that we will end up one day with quality standards that already exist in many provinces, but we will reach them at different rates. That is another foundation of the policy put forward by the Party, that we respect the rate at which each province progresses.
It is clear that Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland have different rates of growth for a social product or program. One only has to look at a province's wealth and existing services, how developed its education services are, what work opportunities there are. Because of all that, the rate and support. . . support at that rate will start for a national program, and that is important for federal programs. All the policies we put forward, that sometimes lay in a grey area between federal and provincial jurisdictions, always led us to respect provincial rates of action, and this is what makes this Government different.
In my first year here, Mr. Speaker, I was Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Hon. Flora MacDonald, with whom I worked more closely at that time. We opened negotiations with the Province of Quebec, among others, on training programs. You are fully aware training programs are a long-standing contending issue between federal and provincial Governments, training being a provincial matter. Our greatest difficulty was to somewhat make up for the past because we were dealing with provinces that had been irked to the limit by standards that had always been forced upon them by the Canadian Government, because it had the spending power, it was at the top, it knew about all the needs, and had the means.
We succeeded in harmonizing and setting up new programs, a new job strategy ensuring that instead of having programs strictly to distribute the money to the people, we put forward programs that still sent the money to the people but that led the people to better themselves. Such has been the new job strategy, and the same job strategy was developed among students where the priority is to favour jobs that suit the student's career profile.
But the same thing applies to child care services. Ontario and Quebec will develop their own quality standards. They will not be all that different, but basically different. And what makes this country great is the fact that we have ten provinces and two territories each one as important as the other, each one having its priorities and its standards. There will be

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
fundamental differences between them but they will remain consistent with the general principles we care to set. And they will be encouraged.
We therefore support a system which will give parents the opportunity to help others, to tell them: Listen, in the field of child care, we are experts. Come and see us. We will take care of everything because we know what you really want.
That is the big difference and, as far as I am concerned, I am all for it. We could even pass it tonight. I am speaking, of course, of Bill C-144.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the second reading debate on Bill C-144, an Act to provide child care to Canada. This is one of those Bills on which we have had an indication with respect to which form outweighs substance.
The Minister has portrayed the Bill as a bold new initiative. He has said that he is making great forays into assisting the families of Canada. As we looked at what he is proposing and as we looked at the kind of family assistance that his Government has provided we began to form quite a different opinion of what the Government is doing for families.
Over the years we have watched the previous Liberal Government and then this Conservative Government continue the practice of reducing the proportion of the family deductions on the income tax form. At one time those deductions would feed and clothe a child. That is what their original intention was. As the years went by that was eroded to the point now where, for most families, the child deduction barely provides the clothing that they need each year. This is the same group of people who are in the defence of the Canadian family.
In my home province of Saskatchewan they fought medicare, one of the programs that probably did as much as anything to provide equal access to full medical care for young people, old people, members of families, whether they could afford to see a doctor, be hospitalized or have a serious expensive operation. Medicare made that possible. It was both Liberals and Conservatives in our province who fought the introduction of that program.
During the past four years we have watched this Government attempt successfully-211 outvote 70-to deindex family allowances, further eroding the spending power of families. The provisions of family allowance have been in place since 1948-49. They were introduced as an attempt to equalize incomes and make poorer families more equal, give them access to goods and services on a more equal basis with the rest of the country's families. This is the Government that deindex-ed family allowances. It is also the Government that has gone
a long way in increasing taxes on ordinary families, particularly those families who find it necessary for both mom and dad to work.
The other day I did some quick calculations. A family with mom, dad, two kids, and both parents working most of the time, earning in the neighbourhood of $35,000, and a great many of our population are earning that type of salary and less, with the discovery by the Government of the ease with which it can extract taxes from ordinary people by increasing sales tax, that family is now paying more than $1,000 per year more in taxes than four years ago before the Government came to power. This Government purports to be the Government that stands up for families, yet it is taking more than $100 a month from the average working family with two children.
It is an unfortunate reality that a great many of our population is in the position where both mother and father have to work for wages. When we look at the statistics it can be seen that there are 856,000 two-parent families where both parents work. If either of those parents stopped working to stay home to devote all their time to child care and raising the family, the family income would go below the poverty line. Working mothers and fathers are not only a reality, but in most families they are also a necessity.
I wish to spend a little time talking about the special needs of the farm families that I know best, many of whom I represent in a rural riding such as I have. They will find any federal or provincial program suspicious, because they are not certain that their needs for child care will be recognized in any program that has been proposed. These farm families may be described by some people as traditional families, and to the untrained observer it may appear that the mother is not working. However, I assure you Mr. Speaker, that all farm wives probably have the equivalent of two or three jobs. They contribute not only to the income and the labour force required on the farm, but they are also required to look after the children. The main child-rearing role still falls on farm mothers. Farm fathers help as much as they can, but they are engaged in what are generally too dangerous pursuits in which to include children.
While farms are great places to raise children, and I would not have chosen to raise mine anywhere else, they can also be very dangerous places to raise children. Every season I hear of terrible accidents where young children, sometimes as old as 10 years old, but usually 10 and younger, are killed in the most horrible farm accidents that occurred largely because there was no supervision for them, or no one to help look after them. The parents were too busy trying to earn a living to keep full track of the children, or they were trying to involve them in some of the farm activities where an accident resulted.
We all know of instances where children have been inadvertently run over by a tractor. There are also combine or baler
accidents where they become entangled in power shafts. Not
August 23, 1988

too many years ago in my neighbourhood there was an incident where a fairly old child of nine or ten fell into a load of flax as it was being unloaded out of a 10-inch auger. He was immediately drowned. Flax flows like water and it was impossible to extract him. We also know of unfortunate incidents with manure pits around hog barns. There are sewage lagoons in some farm yards where open pits are still used for disposal of sewage. Most farms have ponds, dug-outs, or dams where it is possible for children to get into trouble. It is especially worrisome to parents in the busy times of the year when there is seeding or harvest time when mother and father are involved, as well as the older children, in trying to get the harvest in. Sometimes the children are on their own.
Any program proposed under a day care system, and I do not see any reference to it in this particular proposal, has to be flexible, accessible, affordable, and available in those small rural communities. The type of day care system that will fit those needs has not been attacked by this program or, I submit, most of the programs that I have seen. I do admit that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Collins), does have a section in her policy where she is at least prepared to put some money, study, and action into experiments in the rural areas to establish the workable day care and child care system that can work in those outlying, scattered rural communities where the population is scattered, but where the need is very great.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-144, the so-called day care Bill. I say the "so-called day care Bill" because this Bill is not a day care Bill. It is a "promise" care Bill. It is an attempt to care for the promises made by the Government four years ago when it first sought office as a governing Party, and when it promised a comprehensive, adequate, and accessible day care program for Canada.
Anyone who understands the need for day care today, accessible, quality day care, or anyone who has any idea of what is required and who is able to read this Bill, in either official language, will quickly discover that there is no relationship between the need that continues to grow as the nature of our economy evolves, and what is delivered in this Bill.
The country needs, and is going to need, some 2 million day care spaces. The Bill delivers 200,000 day care spaces over the next seven years. The requirement is for 2 million. The Bill delivers at best 200,000. The Bill does not recognize that society has dramatically changed in the past 20 years. Today less than one in six Canadian families fit the traditional view and pattern of the wife at home with the children and the husband off working. Many families today are headed by single parents, and most of those parents are single young mothers. While more than half of all women with pre-school children work outside the home, only about 20 per cent, two in ten, of those children are served by an accredited day care centre. Raising children is more expensive than ever before,
Canada Child Care Act
whether one or both parents work, and providing child care is one of the highest costs.
This Bill fails to recognize the tremendous need in the country today. Indeed, there is an excellent editorial in The Ottawa Citizen by Marjorie Nichols. The headline was "Epp"-referring to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp)-"at last decides his figures for child care program". It is an excellent article. It points out that one should get past the flimflammery. Once you have shattered the mirrors, once you have blown away the smoke, once you have seen through the orchestrated series of press events and numbers, you can see that the country does not have a child care program.
In 1966 medicare was established in this country. It worked because the national Government of the day, I am pleased to say a Liberal Government, established a set of national standards, established the principle that whether you are a Canadian living in British Columbia, Toronto, Montreal, Quebec City, Saskatoon or in St. Anthony, Newfoundland, your access to medical care, the kind of standard that you could expect as a Canadian, one of the qualifiers, one of the things that we held in common no matter where we lived, was a level of medical care that would be consistent right across this land. We set national standards. It was a national social program.
Nowhere in Bill C-144, the so-called day care Bill, is there anything establishing any national standard whatever across this country. Nowhere is there any guarantee that if you live in St. Anthony, Newfoundland, to the extent that you look to your federal Government because you are a citizen of Canada and your access to day care will be equivalent to the access of someone who lives in Toronto, Ontario, by comparison a much wealthier province, you will have those standards. They are not there, Mr. Speaker.
What is more shocking and what most Canadians do not realize is that there is absolutely nothing in this Bill to ensure that if you live in St. Anthony, Newfoundland, in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia or in Manitoba or, for that matter if you live in Ontario, your province will even participate in a national day care program. Indeed, this Bill makes it not only possible but I would submit plausible, if not likely, that we will see those provinces with the fiscal capacity to participate in the program to the extent it meets any of the needs, but will do so only at a level of about 10 per cent, and we will see those without a fiscal capacity to participate not sign on board. Some provinces will determine that their fiscal capacity and priorities are in other directions and Canadians in some provinces of Canada will not be participating in this day care program.
We in this Party insist upon national, enforceable standards, similar to what we have in medicare. I heard my colleague in the New Democratic Party who just spoke, a Member from western Canada, refer to his own Party's day care proposal. He

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
said with respect to rural Canada-I represent a rural constituency-that his own Party's program makes some attempt and shows some willingness to experiment to see whether or not we can provide some services to rural Canadians. Ele said quite rightly that rural Canadians are very suspicious about day care policies no matter from which Party they come. They have this notion that we are talking about young, upwardly mobile professional working couples who can afford things like day care.
Like the Member from Hamilton East.

There is really nothing for rural Canadians because in rural Canada the vast majority of day care in rural Newfoundland, almost all day care, is provided in home by people who open their homes and establish, in almost all cases that I know of, a quality level of day care for couples who are working or for a single mother who requires day care. The New Democratic Party's proposal makes no provision for that kind of day care.
The NDP proposal does not have the flexibility to develop that kind of day care. The NDP proposal wants to institutionalize right across this country a model based on a model that works perfectly in Toronto-God bless Toronto.
Rural Canadians need access-not to tax deductions because if your income is low you cannot claim it anyway-to tax credits. That has to be part of the proposal. While I fundamentally do not disagree with my friends in the New Democratic Party, who share many of the concerns the Liberal Party feels about this Bill and who recognize many of its gaping flaws, we must deal with the reality of Canada as we find it. We cannot afford the luxury as we develop laws and social policy for this nation of living in a false Utopia concocted by some pollster or academic living in an ivory tower in some fabled urban setting. We must recognize-

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to join in the debate on this important issue of child care for Canadian families. It is my pleasure to participate because I do have some very important things to say which I think will outline the total inadequacy of the Government's approach to this issue. In doing so I want to talk about the kind of families that we mean when we talk about families in Canada.
I am sure this Government has no idea what most people in this country need because it probably did not ask the families themselves what kinds of needs they have. There are approximately 16,000 families in my riding of St. John's East with children living at home. That is comparable to other ridings
across this country. In my riding of 16,000 families, 3,600 of them are single parent families. Over 20 per cent are single parent families who are living in a situation where there is not a Mom and a Pop and two kids and two incomes and all those things that a lot of people take for granted when they talk about child care. We have to look at a program that meets the needs of single parent families, of two parent families, of situations where everything is not straightforward and even where two parents are working and where those kinds of choices which the Minister keeps talking about may or may not be available.
What we need to recognize is that for families who have children to look after and who need to work the biggest issue in their lives is how to find affordable quality child care. I know that from contact with people in those kinds of situations who have to struggle from one situation to the next who cannot find quality child care, who cannot find care they can afford and with which they can be satisfied and comfortable.
We heard the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) who spoke about what a wonderful situation she had as an upper middle-class Canadian in a two-parent working family. She was able to find this caregiver who was adequate and provided quality care. That is a marvellous and a wonderful thing. It is a situation which could adequately operate under a New Democratic Party child care proposal. It is a situation where an individual, a caregiver, can associate with a licensed facility, be given assistance to provide quality care in terms of facilities and equipment for caregiving, and in terms of ensuring that that caregiver is given an adequate income.
That is the kind of flexibility that our Party would support and has proposed. It would provide quality and would be affordable, not only to the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mrs. Dewar), who has indicated that she makes an income quite substantially higher than that of the vast majority of Canadians, but for average working men and women who have to look after their children. They too should be able to afford quality care, and should be able to exercise a choice. The situation of a woman who is at home and is already looking after one or two children would quite adequately be met by providing assistance to the care giver at that level to ensure quality care giving as well as an adequate income for the care giver. Those are the kinds of choices our policy represents.
The Government suggests that one of the choices available to this mythical family composed of mom, pop and the kids is whether to work or not to work. The choice goes something like this: "We will give you a child tax credit of $200 per year if you decide to stay at home and look after your own children at home". Of course, that amounts to $ 16.66 a month. This is a real choice. I can see the women of Canada for the next three weeks mulling over whether or not to quit their jobs, stay at home and look after their children for the sake of $16.66 a
August 23, 1988

month. Those are the kinds of choices that are in the proposal the Government has put forward.
We would provide a national child care system which has a number of essential characteristics including accountability to parents. The child care system would be established on a nonprofit basis. Those who are already involved in profit-making centres would agree to a transition period for setting up nonprofit centres with control by parents and the care givers themselves. That would be desirable because this is a basic and fundamental service which meets a basic social need. It should be met on a non-profit basis. Most of the people who are now involved in child-care giving on a for-profit basis would do better in terms of personal income under a non-profit system based on the proposal of the New Democratic Party.
The essential features of such a system would be the requirement of minimum standard applicable all across Canada, specifically training standards and parent and community ownership and control of non-profit services. This would provide quality, affordable services. The next requirement would be that the system be accessible, that it would be available to those in St. Anthony, Newfoundland, as well as to those in Toronto. Parents need access to the kind of care that is standardized, provided that care givers are licensed so that parents will have some assurance that the people providing the service do adhere to training standards and are trustworthy and acceptable people.
Those elements are essential to a proper child care program. They are all missing from the Government's program. There is an absence of national objectives. There is no vision in the offering of child care choices that are needed. In fact, it imposes restrictions on the increases in child care spaces. It does not allow for an expanding and developing market, and for the first time has imposed restrictions on the amount of government assistance that will be offered to child care workers. This makes it impossible for us to support the Government's Bill. It does not do anything to enhance the position of child care workers, positions which are at best marginalized by the policies which allow for individuals to use the tax system to pay people minimum wages or less to look after children across Canada. That itself speaks for low standards and does not do anything to increase the quality of training and care.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Hawkes (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, truth comes in strange ways and at strange moments. I think my colleague across the way just laid a little truth on the table. I think he said that they are against the Bill because it does nothing for child care workers. Does he mean all child care workers? Does he mean babysitters, the teenagers who sit for other people's children, the friends and neighbours? Are these child care workers? Are mothers child care workers?
I suspect that the NDP definition of a child care worker is someone who works in an institution and belongs to some kind of association which verges on being a union. Whether it is free
Canada Child Care Act
trade or child care, the NDP represents a leadership element in Canadian society. It represents people with pretty big salaries, union leaders, who drive pretty big cars and travel to pretty good hotels. The behaviour of Members across the way is conditioned on behalf of those people, the union leaders who belong to their political Party. It is time for them to join the rest of us in speaking out on behalf of all Canadians, not just a small portion of Canadians who happen to be in that fortunate position but on behalf of all Canadians.
The child care policy of this Government is a policy on behalf of all children, children who are cared for in their homes by their mothers or fathers. We are offering some help for them to raise their children. This legislation deals with the provisions of child care services in a more formal sense. The basic philosophy of this piece of legislation is that Parliament will provide money to the provinces to set up the services which the provinces need for the people who live in those provinces.
Living in Tuktoyaktuk is not the same as living in downtown Toronto. Living in Barrhead, Alberta, is not the same as living in the City of Calgary. What the NDP and Liberal Members are asking for when they talk about national standards is some kind of minimum qualification for the workers in the system, not for the good of the children. Children are well cared for by parents, no formal schooling required. They give love, care and attention. Children are well cared for by teenagers. Children are well cared for by relatives, by friends, by neighbours
Not always, they aren't.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
"Not always", she shouts across. They are not always well cared for by licensed, accredited child care workers or teachers or university professors. She knows that and I know that. We belong to that profession, and some of our colleagues go wrong. Some of them do terrible things. Some of them end up in jail. There is nothing legislation can do to ensure the quality of people, but we can tell the parents of Canada that they must accept some responsibility for determining whether the care their children are about to receive is the kind of care that they value. Is it consistent with your personal attitude and philosophy? This Bill encourages that kind of choice. This Bill says that we will enter into an agreement with the provinces to provide money to meet the child care needs in those provinces. This will be done in a way that fits.
What the NDP is saying is, let us let the population centres of the country decide, the areas with the most MPs, Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, places with high density apartment buildings, lots of jobs in manufacturing, and a certain kind of lifestyle. They produce the most MPs because most people live in those kinds of centres, and the bulk of those MPs shall decide on a standard for the rest of the nation; for a fishing village in Newfoundland; a prairie agricultural community; a northern mining town. Let us have a standard that fits the cities. It may not fit the children but it fits workers because

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
you can control the supply and raise the wages of those who are lucky enough to be inside the system.
That is what the NDP represents. NDP Members would have you believe that they can produce a day care program which meets the same goals of this program for less money in virtually half the time. That proposition is an absolute joke. First, because the federal Government has no business in the day care business. It has no jurisdiction under Canadian law and the Canadian Constitution to run a day care system. In the same way it has no jurisdiction to run the public education system. Our forefathers gave that jurisdiction to the provinces so the politicians would be closer to the people when dealing with human and health services.
As a federal Government we can contribute. We can recognize a need and provide money. How can the NDP propose to do, for less money in a shorter period of time, more than what is proposed in this legislation? Have they had a single consultation with a single province? Have they been out there discussing with the provinces their needs, their priorities, their capacity? The NDP intends to provide all the money because this Bill does not provide all the money. The people of a province put up some of the money and the federal Government puts up some of the money. It is a partnership so that the program remains sensitive to the needs of the people in the province.
That is a long, slow process. We lived through 17 years of government where the Parliament of Canada thought it could intrude on provincial jurisdiction and do what it liked. We brought a different spirit to this land. We said we will come to office in a spirit of co-operation. Let the federal Government be the helpmate of the provinces. Let us discuss, let us work it out, let us avoid duplication, let us save taxpayers' dollars by co-operating and building together.
If the results of all those consultations and this legislation is to produce 200,000 new day care spaces for this dollar amount over a period of seven years, it does so because the consultation process has produced information from the provinces about their capacity, their needs and their willingness to proceed. Without that consultation with respect to doing something in an area of provincial jurisdiction you are simply saying to the Canadian people: "I have an idea. It is a pie in the sky idea but hopefully some of it will stick. It is not based on facts. It is not based on reality. Hopefully Canadians will believe me".
I think Canadians have their feet on the ground. I think Canadians know how much time and effort it takes to set up a new organization, a collection of parents, to create a new day care centre with a good board, good constitution, good facilities and adequate staff. Those things take months. You cannot stand in Parliament, decree it to happen and expect it to be there the next day. These are community endeavours of some complexity requiring participation on a voluntary basis by a lot of people.
The organizations that exist today to help are provincial Governments and the departments of those provincial Governments. They have the staff on a daily basis working with these kinds of groups. They know how long it takes. They know how expensive it is. I say to Canadians: When it comes to child care you really have a choice. In the next election you can vote for the Party who cares about their child care workers and their union bosses, or you can vote for the Party who cares about children and parental choice.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have a chance to speak on Bill C-144, the Canada Child Care Act. There is no question that this is a very important subject to literally millions of young couples who have children of school age or pre-school children. We learn as we look across the statistics that 44 per cent of families have two careers. Some 63 per cent of all mothers who work today, two million women, have children under 16 years of age. Almost half of all the women with pre-school children require day care.
What we need is an accessible, high quality, affordable day care system. Although we have some 250,000 licensed day care spaces today, the actual need approaches some two million across the country. There are lots of problems with the present system under CAP which is operated through the provinces. It is not very satisfactory for those in the middle income group because it is a welfare system. If you are above a certain level of income you cannot utilize it. Of course, other private day care systems are just too expensive for those middle income families.
The whole system today is not adequate to deal with the situation as we see it in rural Canada. Farming communities and resource areas certainly do not have an adequate day care system. The shortages are growing worse every year.
The plan before us today is an interesting one because when it was announced last December it was $1 billion less. There was a famous cabinet Minister who said: "What's a million"? In this case the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), who has probably at his disposal more computers, more technical back up, than any other Department of government, erred by $1 billion. He announced a program of $5.3 billion. He discovered four or five months later that he was $1 billion short. The interesting part of that is that if we read the article written just a couple days ago in The Ottawa Citizen by Marjorie Nichols, the program put forward by the Government, involving some $4 billion for actual day care service itself, if you extrapolate it out over the seven year period, actually amounts to $570,000 per year above what is being paid out by the Government now under the Canada Assistance Plan. That takes into account inflation over the seven years. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, how much less it was before he added the $1 billion.
So we really have a proposal before us which probably will
not do anything different from what we have under the present
system. Of course, provinces that opt into this new proposal
August 23, 1988

will have to opt out of the Canada Assistance Program permanently. So we have a very questionable system which has already proven it is $1 billion short. The whole proposal is based on the provinces picking up this $4 billion. If the provinces do not have their share, then, of course, the $4 billion will not be spent.
There are a lot of problems with this proposal. First, there is no proposal to have national standards. So even if one has a rinky-dink system, one still receives the money because there are no national standards established by this program. There is very little help for the mother who stays at home. In fact, in this fiscal year, as I understand the proposal, they receive exactly a SI00 refundable tax credit. Next year it will be $200. The Hon. Member opposite, who is shaking his head and who raves every day about the socialists, may think $200 is enough to allow a homemaker to stay at home and take care of the children, but anyone who stops to think about it can see it is obviously not enough. That is why our distinguished critic, who served on the committee, proposed refundable spousal deduction. It is not only a tax credit but it is a refundable tax credit. If the deduction for a spouse is now, say, $4,000, and the tax credit basis is at 30 per cent or 40 per cent, they would receive that as a refundable tax credit in their own hands. If the spouse is not working or does not have any other income, she still receives the income. So there is an incentive there for homemakers and mothers to stay at home and raise their children, especially during the pre-school years.
The present system, which is going through the tax reform now in the Bill before the House, increases the exemption from $2,000 to $4,000 per year. Of course, it is a very regressive system. It is much more advantageous if one is in a high-income bracket. The New Democratic Party wants to cut that out. The NDP thinks it should only be maintained at the $2,000 limit. That is even more regressive because it does not provide the assistance for those who want to stay home.
What is more important, the proposal before the House does not carry enough new spaces. We need at least a million spaces. This proposal only creates 200,000 new spaces over a period of seven years. The system does not equitably share the burden. There should be more assistance for those low-income families.
We believe that this proposal, although it may have some useful features to it, it is not adequate. It simply does not meet the need. It is regressive. It is unfair and, most of all, it does not really provide a great deal of new money. According to Marjorie Nichols, who writes a column for The Citizen, over the life of the seven year program only $570,000 per year of new money is added. I think we have a very inadequate proposal before us tonight. It may be $570,000 better per year than the present system, but surely that is not a massive new national day care program. We know it is not. It does not provide much extra money and it does not provide any national standards. It is simply inadequate to deal with the massive responsibility which is before the country. It just does not adequately meet the needs of young families who cannot
Canada Child Care Act
afford proper day care when, because of economic necessity, both members of the family, both parents, have to work outside the home.

Mr. Speaker, the question of providing an adequate day care system is of crucial importance to the people of Canada. The fact is that 60 per cent of the mothers of children under the age of three are now in the workforce. Most of these mothers are not just single parent mothers, but mothers in families with a joint income where both the husband and wife are working and mothers in families where both mother and father are middle-income earners who are working.
Why is that happening, Mr. Speaker? Well, to a large extent it is because it is almost impossible for a young couple to buy their own home and meet the mortgage payments with only one member of the family working. This is true even in the City of Winnipeg where the price of a home is probably just one-half of what it is in Ottawa, or a third of the cost of a home in Vancouver and probably a quarter of the cost of a home in Toronto. In the newer parts of my constituency the people who live there are almost entirely young couples between the ages of 25 and 40 years. One could shoot off a cannon during the middle of the day and there would not be a single person come out of the house to see what was happening because there is no one home. Both husband and wife are out working so they can meet the mortgage payments.
So Members of Parliament or people out in the community who believe and talk about really having a choice should realize that the choice for most parents is some system of day care or home care. They just do not realize what is happening. The choice is no longer between day care, public or private, adequate or inadequate, and home care, because home care is no longer a viable, possible choice. The alternative to day care is some kind of arrangement, leaving the child with a neighbour or getting some high school student in to look after the children or getting someone from the Philippines or some other country to come and look after the child, and these parents have no knowledge at all about the adequacy or ability of that person to give careful care and supervision of the children.
These are the facts. What are the needs? Health and Welfare Canada, which is not a preserve of wild-eyed radicals by any stretch of the imagination, states that the number of children with parents working more than 20 hours a week is over two million. According to Health and Welfare Canada, there are presently only 250,000 child care spaces. That means there are 1.75 million children of working parents for whom there are no child care spaces.
I find it amazing that Conservative Members of Parliament who talk so glibly and often about the family and how much they care about the family are prepared to ignore the problem or bring forth a proposal to deal with the problem that is

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
completely inadequate. It simply does not meet the needs of the people.
If one listens to the Parliamentary Secretary who spoke a few moments ago, one would think that the proposals put forward by members of the NDP are impractical, unaffordable and were somehow pulled out of thin air.
I want to put on the record the principles of a national day care policy as enunciated, not by the New Democratic Party, but by the Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association. They say about universality:
All children should have access to high quality child care services regardless of family income or parent's employment status. Parents should determine the nature and extent of their children's participation.
They say about quality:
To ensure high quality, child care services should be licensed and regulated, reflecting the best current knowledge about early childhood development as well as the varied cultural and linguistic backgrounds of Canadian families.
One need only drive through the core areas of the major cities in Canada to see that the days when the population of the cities was 95 per cent white are long gone. In some of the core areas in the City of Winnipeg, for example, 95 per cent of the children attending elementary school are either immigrant children from Caribbean countries and South America or native children. They must have a care system that meets their needs, not one that is dictated to them by a government from Ottawa. They need a system that is developed in consultation with the local community and parents.
The Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association discusses affordability. It states:
Cost should not be a barrier to access for any family. User fees should diminish over a realistic time frame, with a small parent fee to remain. Assistance with this fee should be provided to low-income families.
We know that there are many low income families in the cities. Unfortunately, there is an increasing number of low income families in rural areas.
The Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association says about working conditions:
Child care staff should receive salaries and benefits commensurate with the value of their work and educational qualifications.
Let us deal with the question of cost and how we will pay for it.
We believe the federal Conservative Government has rejected the principles of organizations such as the one I just referred to, and has rejected the very fundamental principles it advocated when it urged Canadians to support the Meech Lake Accord.
Let us consider how these programs will be financed. Of the almost S5.5 billion being committed by the federal Government to the program, almost S2.5 billion will be spent through the tax system. Day care advocates and the former Manitoba Government estimated that if this had been committed to
creating new services, another 170,000 spaces could have been created for day care.
A large percentage of the almost $5.5 billion that the Government says it proposes to allocate to day care facilities is not new money. The federal Government presently spends $170 million every year through the child care expense deduction. Thus this would come to approximately $1 billion in new money.
Furthermore, the larger percentage of the money being proposed by the Government is going into a doubling of the child tax deduction. The Government's program already gives the greatest benefit to well-to-do families and gives nothing to low income families. That should be of no surprise because since day one, after its election, the Government has demonstrated quite clearly that it believes in the trickle-down theory of economics, that if you only give enough to people at the top through large salaries and tax breaks on investments or capital gains, the money spent by those with high income will somehow trickle down to those in the lower income brackets. That has not worked before and it will not work now.
Less well-off families will be given an increase of $100 for the first year for the child tax credit and a further $100 in the second year for baby-sitting or parents at home. A $200 increase is absolutely meaningless in terms of giving women real choices. If they are wealthy, $200 means nothing. Those who are in the lower income bracket need a great deal more than $200.
We have made it very clear that the Government's proposals are simply inadequate. We have proposed an alternative that meets the criteria and principles enunciated by organizations such as the one I have mentioned and by people who work in the existing day care centres who know the needs of the children who are in their care.
I, along with my colleagues, intend to oppose this legislation and do everything I can to see a much better system in place that will meet the needs of Canadian children.
