According to the Minister of State it is probably $200 million. It is a very substantial amount. I ask myself what the devil is going on.

The Liberal Party finance critic states that dividends would be taxed at a lower rate than capital gains and that companies would thus be discouraged from reinvesting their profits into their business. What he did not say, however, was that if the capital gains tax is higher than the tax on dividends, perhaps the tax on dividends should be adjusted then to ensure greater equity with respect to the capital gains tax. What he failed to state was that it is impossible to accept that about 14 per cent of the population still lives below the poverty line. Tax reform is supposed to lower the taxes of low-income earners. Here we have the Liberal Party that wants to lower the taxes of those realizing capital gains . . . and who is going to pay? In the final analysis the ordinary taxpayer is going to pay.
Mr. Speaker, I see that only 1 per cent of the Canadian population realized 38 per cent of all capital gains in 1983. Who are these individuals? They are people who earn in excess of $100,000 a year. The mesure proposed by the Liberal Party finance critic would also affect large corporations. Instead of ensuring that corporations will pay their fair share of taxes, the Liberal Party wants the capital gains tax to be even lower than that proposed by the Conservative Party. The New Democratic Party believes that the other two parties are wrong. The Liberals are wrong in wanting to favour individuals and corporations realizing capital gains. The Conservatives are also wrong in trying to retain certain privileges for the wealthy and for corporations, in so far as capital gains are concerned.
I do not understand what the devil is going on. However, I noticed that, according to Statistics Canada, the poverty line

August 23, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
in 1988 for a family of four in a major Canadian city is approximately $23,400. The Conservative tax reform will tax that family when its income exceeds $18,500, or $5,000 below the poverty line. The Conservative tax reform gives tax cuts of over $4,000 to the largest number of people with incomes of over $100,000 a year. It is essentially unfair because it taxes people in poverty and gives big returns and big reductions in tax to people with high incomes.
What did the Liberals do about it? Did they try to ensure that the tax not be paid by people living below the poverty line? No. Did they try to ensure that tax be paid at least at current levels by people earning big incomes? No. What the Liberals tried to do is bring down the tax even further on wealthy Canadians, and bring down the tax even further on wealthy corporations, and not do a thing for ordinary taxpayers living below the poverty line.
As things presently stand under the outgoing tax system, the maximum rate for an individual of tax on capital gains is 17 per cent. At two-thirds inclusion under the new system it will be raised to 19 per cent. That is pretty dramatic, and a really substantial tax reform. The Liberals are saying that capital gains are so acceptable that they should continue to be privileged and only have a tax rate of 2 per cent more than was being paid under the old system, while at the same time a technician working for Bell Canada will pay a tax rate only two or three points below the tax rate paid by Jean de Grand-pre who has a million dollar income as a CEO and President of Bell Canada. There is something wrong with that.
A wealthy Canadian will pay 19 per cent of the value of his or her capital gains, according to the Liberal amendment, whereas the average Canadian, who is struggling to pay a mortgage, struggling to pay high interest rates, and struggling to support his or her family, will wind up paying 8 per cent more in tax on a marginal income of over $27,000 a year.
I cannot accept that type of Liberal tax reform. It reminds me that over the last year while the finance committee has been working on this particular issue, we have been trying to clean up problems and loopholes in the tax system which were put there first by the Liberals, particularly when the present Leader of the Liberal Party was the Minister of Finance, and also by the Progressive Conservatives in the rare periods of time when they had a chance to put loopholes into the tax system. If a certain company wanted a privilege, of course that was available; if wealthy Canadians wanted capital gains to be treated differently, of course it was available. That was the Liberal policy, and that was the Conservative policy.
Canadian voters who look at the two Parties in the forthcoming election campaign should remember precisely that. The Liberals take their marching orders from wealthy Canadians and corporations, just as the Progressive Conservatives take their marching orders from the same sources. If the Royal Bank gives $50,000 to the Conservatives, it gives $50,000 to the Liberals. Who will benefit from the new treatment of capital gains? The Royal Bank will be one of the
beneficiaries. If Alcan Aluminum wants to go for years without paying any tax at all, then it supports the Liberal Party. Alcan was allowed to go for years paying no tax at all. Now its favours turn over to the Progressive Conservatives, because who failed to put a minimum tax on corporations? Why, the Progressive Conservatives. Under the Reagan tax reform in the United States a minimum tax exists. It cannot be that progressive a measure if it was brought in by the Reaga-nites in Washington. However, the Tories did not bring that in here. The Liberals allowed Alcan, and many other companies, to go without paying tax at all.
Now on the side of capital gains, the Liberals are standing up to be counted. When you stand up to be counted on this issue, Mr. Speaker, you stand with ordinary Canadians, or you stand with corporations and wealthy Canadians.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) stands with wealthy Canadians and corporations because his Party is going to continue to treat capital gains favourably. Right at the side of the Minister of State for Finance stands the finance critic for the Liberal Party, and all of his Party. That Party is attempting to outdo the Conservatives in seeking support from the corporate sector by saying: "Look, we are not going to tax your capital gains the way those nasty Conservatives were going to do it. We are going to tax them less".
It reminds me of the marketing battles between Steinberg's and Loblaw's. Those stores kept having to reduce their prices in order to bring customers into the stores. We all know that the Liberals have been having trouble raising corporate donations over the last three or four years, and that is why that Party is $5 million in debt. It seems to me that what the Liberals are saying is: "Here is a bargain sale. Can you afford not to support us? We will do what you want us to do for you, just make sure that you do what we want you to do for us". The Liberals are saying: "If you support the Liberals, if a corporation makes donations to the Liberal Party, then the Liberal Party will return the favour by ensuring that the days of loopholes and tax exemptions will be here again if the Liberals get a chance to get back in power".
On behalf of my Party, I stand with ordinary Canadians who say that we need a fair tax system which does away with privileges to wealthy Canadians and to corporations.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the position taken by my colleague, the Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), in opposition to this amendment. One of the most important studies made of the tax system in Canada was done by the Royal Commission appointed by Prime Minister Diefenbaker when he was the Leader of the Conservative Party. That commission was chaired by a very distinguished member of the chartered accountant profession in Canada. It made a very important recommendation. It was put before the people and the Government and the Parliament of Canada, Kenneth Carter. It was a very important principle which they believed should be adopted, and that was that a dollar of income is a dollar regardless of how the income is obtained, and every dollar of income should be taxed in the same way, whether it was earned by somebody working for wages or salary, whether it was earned by somebody who was clipping coupons from the bonds or the stocks which he or she earned, or whether it was earned in the form of rents on property which people or corporations owned.
Liberal and Conservative Governments from that day on have ignored and hidden from the public that recommendation made by the Royal Commission headed by Mr. Carter. Let me put on the record what we have seen in the last 35 or more years. In 1954, the federal Government collected in income tax from individuals $1.17 billion. That is eleven thousand million dollars. It got just under that, $1 billion from corporations. That is, it got almost equal amounts of revenue from individual taxpayers and from corporations.
If you look down the road, in 1982 the Liberals had been in office for almost two-thirds of the time from 1952, which I used as a starting point, to 1982. In 1982, the federal Government collected $26 billion in personal income tax and only $8 billion in corporate income tax. We have heard a great deal from the Liberal and Conservative Parties about their desire to move to a fairer tax system. We have heard the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) talking today about what the
Conservatives have accomplished in the way of a fairer tax system, tax reform in reality. What kind of tax reform have we had? The fact is that the average family is now paying somewhere between $1,000 and $1,200 more in taxes. If you include income tax, sales tax, excise tax and certain other taxes, they are paying $1,000 to $1,200 more in 1988 than they paid in 1984 when the Conservative Government was elected.
We talked about corporation taxes. My colleague, the Member for Ottawa Centre, has already pointed out that an employee of Bell Canada earning between $20,000 and $30,000 a year will pay income tax at a rate only a few percentage points lower than the rate paid by the head of Bell Canada, Mr. de Grandpre, whose salary is over $1 million a year. That is how this Government looks at the tax system. That is what this Government means when it talks about its tax reform bases.
Let us just look at what has happened to corporation taxes. We know that small businesses-most of them individually owned-are paying a pretty healthy amount in the form of corporation taxes. When we look at the record for the last fiscal year for which we have information supplied to us by Revenue Canada, we see that in the year 1986 some of the most profitable, largest corporations in Canada somehow paid no tax at all.
Alcan Aluminum, whose pre-tax income was over $306 million, paid not one cent in corporation tax. Brascan had profits of $186 million and paid no tax at all. Power Financial which had profits of $131 million paid no tax at all. Hees International had profits of $117 million and paid not one penny in tax. Xerox Canada had $115 million in profits and paid not one cent in income tax. Cadillac Fairview, one of the most successful real estate developers in this country, had profits of $95 million in 1986 and paid not one cent in tax. Bramalea, another real estate developer, had profits of over $50 million and paid not one cent in taxes.
We have to ask ourselves from where is this Government coming? What has happened to its promises about tax reform? What has happened to the promise of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in the debates held just before the election that he agreed individuals and corporations should pay a minimum tax? As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre pointed out a few moments ago, the United States with the most conservative President, the most conservative right-wing administration it has had in the last 50 or more years has imposed a minimum tax on corporations. But this Conservative Government of Canada which talks about tax reform and fairness has not in four years tightened up the tax system so that every corporation, particularly the larger corporations, will be required to pay taxes.
They are only following the example set for them by previous Liberal governments. There was no one more
August 23, 1988

generous to corporations and wealthy individuals in the Liberal government years than the present Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) when he was its Minister of Finance. In his first budget he gave a 9 per cent corporate tax reduction to manufacturing and processing companies. Lie also allowed these companies overly generous depreciation tax deductions on their equipment.
We will oppose this motion. Although we have become accustomed to the Liberals becoming quite progressive when in opposition and being very conservative when in government, here is a case where the Liberals are being very conservative and generous to their big business friends even while in the opposition. Lord only knows what they will do if they ever have a chance to form the government again. They would continue the process this Government has followed of giving more and more concessions to those individuals and corporations which have the most.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to try to throw a little light onto this debate by reminding those viewing and listening to what we have to say in Parliament of the measure that is before us. That is the amendment and the concrete proposal we are dealing with here. What may cause some confusion as people examine the proposal is the rhetoric of each of the parties. Let us examine it. The Liberals and their spokesmen talked about equity and taxation. The Conservative spokesperson talked about democracy in taxation. Our Party is concerned about fairness in the taxation for the ordinary Canadian family.
I want to look behind the rhetoric to see whether or not the actions of each of these Parties stand up to their rhetorical flourishes. Let me begin by looking at the Liberals. When they talk about equity in taxation and we examine their amendment before us today, what are they saying? Equity to me means one person or one group will be treated with equal fairness as another group of people. When it comes to equity, the Liberal definition of equity is pretty narrow. Their spokesman was concerned about whether those who receive income from stocks and bonds, other investments, and dividends be treated equally with those who receive capital gains. That was the narrow definition of equity. At no time when they spoke for equity did they raise the concerns of the ordinary Canadian family.
For those who earn their income from the sweat on their brow, at no time did the Liberals say that person who gets a pay cheque ought to be treated with equity. They said: "We want to take care of those who have stocks, bonds and get dividends and see that they are treated the same as those who have capital gains." I did not hear that spokesperson say we
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
have to be concerned that taxes on the ordinary family have gone up by $1,500 under the Tory Government in the last three or four years and there ought to be some equity for the ordinary Canadian family and for the person who earns his or her income from a salary. While the Liberal Party is calling for taxation on capital gains to be reduced from three-quarters of that gain to two-thirds, the Liberals did not say that the ordinary family, except for a few small deductions, has to pay taxes on the vast majority of its income.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: 100 per cent.

speechtext:
Yes, 100 per cent. The Liberals did not call for a reduction in that area. Why did the amendment not call for that? That is the Liberal definition of equity. It is narrow, limited and shows no concern for the ordinary Canadian family.
What about the Conservative definition of democracy in taxation? The Conservatives say that to forgive taxes on capital gains is okay. It is okay to say that if your capital goes up in value by $100,000 you do not have to pay any taxes on it because that privilege is available to every single Canadian. There are very few taxpayers in my riding who have capital gains of that order. Who are the Conservatives talking for when they speak of democracy and capital gains and taxation? They are talking about giving a loaf to the wealthy while asking the ordinary middle-class Canadian to be satisfied with a few crumbs that fall off the table. In other words, if middle-class Canadians benefit in some small measure from capital gains exemption, they should not be concerned that others gain handsomely from it.
What about fairness for the ordinary Canadian family in the taxation system? How can you possibly give tax relief to the ordinary Canadian family if you are going to allow the very wealthy to get away with paying no tax on capital gains? Why is the Liberal Party asking for the measure to go even further than the Conservative Party is presently moving? This is not fair. This is not equity. This is not democracy.

I think I see an indication from you that my time has run out, Mr. Speaker. I think I have made my point. Let me make it once more. It is shocking that when the Liberals talk about equity, they are only talking about dividends and the very wealthy. They have forgotten the ordinary Canadian family.

Mr. Speaker, August 23, commemorating the Ribbentrop-Molotov Treaty of 1939, is celebrated as Black Ribbon Day in many communities across Canada including my own constituency of Kitchener. On August 23, 1939, Hitler and Stalin divided eastern Europe between themselves with the final outcome being that some 300 million Europeans became enslaved by communism.
I call upon all Hon. Members to wear a Black Ribbon Day ribbon or button proudly to demonstrate that the millions of people imprisoned behind the Iron Curtain are not forgotten. I call upon the Government of Canada to make strong representations to the Soviet Union welcoming the new attitudes behind the words glasnost and perestroika, and to prove that these words are not mere rhetoric.
I call upon Mr. Gorbachev to admit the Soviet guilt at Katyn Forest, to return Eastern Poland, Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia to their rightful self-determination, and to honour the Soviet Union's undertaking at Yalta 44 years ago to allow free, democratic and unfettered elections in all of Soviet occupied Europe.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Port of Thunder Bay faces a very bleak future in the year ahead due to the Government's approach to the shipment of grain through this port. Already 700 grain workers, railway workers and sailors have been laid off in the port. A confidential report indicates that by this time next year, over 1,150 will be laid off as well as those in the Great Lakes ports in the Lower St. Lawrence.
Four of the 13 elevators are shut down. Twenty of the 64 grain ships are idle. Of course, if they are idle for over a year many of them will move out of the Great Lakes system. Projections show as low as four million tonnes being shipped from the port in this crop year, whereas in the past year over 14 million tonnes were shipped. The viability of the port is in question when shipments go below seven million tonnes.
The Government has refused to give any commitment to maintain a reasonable share of shipments through this port. Yet only two months ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a commitment of $164 million for one constituency during the Saint-Jean by-election. I call on the Government to take action to maintain the viability of the Port of Thunder Bay which is an essential and important port in the Great Lakes system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on The National last night we saw a bold escape from East Berlin. Four people swam across the River Spree to freedom in West Berlin expecting to be shot at any moment. These brave individuals were helped on shore by some equally brave West
Berliners while an East German patrol boat was rapidly approaching.
I have been to Berlin, both Berlins, East and West. The difference between them is like the difference between night and day. The feeling in the air in East Berlin is a cold feeling of oppression. The feeling in West Berlin is one we all know well. That feeling is freedom.
This is the feeling that those four brave people will enjoy today and from now on. They were prepared to die for their freedom, a freedom we as Canadians take for granted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Justice. A special committee of the Canadian Bar Association has recommended a parallel justice system for Canada's first citizens. The report reveals that in Saskatchewan a treaty Indian woman is 131 times more likely to end up in jail than a white woman, and that 60 per cent of prison admissions are native, while only 6 per cent of Saskatchewan's population is native.
Would the Minister confirm that across Canada 10 per cent of federal inmates are native even though they make up only 2 per cent of the population, and that this Parliament and this Government have the authority and the responsibility to implement a parallel justice system for Canada's first citizens?

August 23, 1988

officials to examine thoroughly and analyse the report and the statements and recommendations made therein.

speechtext:
The House resumed from Wednesday, August 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp (Provencher) that Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mrs. Martin:
That this question be now put.

Mr. Speaker, in terms of social policy at the national level, there is no need more urgent nor claim more legitimate than a call for a comprehensive child care policy. That is what the people of Canada need. That is what they require and that is precisely what the Conservative Government has failed to deliver.
In my youth, to put it in perspective, the large majority of mothers, wherever they were in our country, whether in the East, central Canada, on the plains of our Prairies or beyond the mountains in British Columbia, worked exclusively within the household. Today not only a majority but a growing majority of mothers work outside the home. It is folly to assume, as the Government seems to be, that history will suddenly reverse itself. The conclusion that we reach for those who care for children, for those who believe and believe genuinely in equality between the sexes, for those who prefer reality to mythology as a guide to public policy, is that we need to be launching in Canada a comprehensive child care program, and we need to be doing it now from coast to coast.
Hear, hear!

Today, fully 60 per cent of the mothers of pre-school children are working outside the home, with no access available to quality child care services for almost two million children of such families. The Government in the face of this reality has presented us not with a national program but a national fraud. The Government has done so not in ignorance of the facts for which some matters of policy might be excusable, but it has done so with full knowledge of the contemporary Canadian reality.
The evidence is all around us. For Members of Parliament of each Party in the House of Commons, from any part of our country, whether we speak to our friends, our neighbours or acquaintances we all understand that the family has changed. We have conventional families, unconventional families, women and men reversing conventional roles. Sometimes the man stays at home to rear the child or children while the woman works out in the market-place. More often than not, as I have just indicated, both partners in the family structure are working outside the home. We know it from our personal experience, but beyond our personal experience we have the evidence, and that too was presented to all Members of the House as a result of the special committee established to look into this question.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) for our Party was an active and caring member of that committee and reported back to our caucus on that committee's findings.
Hear, hear!

I want to cite some of the instances that she has drawn to our attention and to the attention of all members of that committee. Again, I repeat, regardless of their Party they became aware of it during the course of their travels throughout Canada.
What are some of the important and salient matters of fact that this Government ought to have been considering that were drawn to our attention by this report? First, that parents overwhelmingly were saying, wherever they were in Canada, whatever their financial circumstance, that it was almost
August 23, 1988

impossible to still find in Canada, in the latter part of the 1980s, reliable and consistent child care service. Second, some mothers actually reported that they had 10 or more different services for care provided before their child was out of the diaper stage. Third, that it is common-not the exception-to take six months or more to be able to find a child care space for one of your children.
It was reported to this committee in a number of instances that parents have had to resort to finding a name posted somewhere, in a local Becker's store or in a grocery store, with a phone number attached which indicated that they would be willing to provide child care service. We should keep in mind that for many families in our country both members are still working outside the home, in part as a matter of choice and also as a matter of economic necessity. If they were not working outside of the home-both partners-the percentage of Canadian families living at the poverty level would rise dramatically.
It is very easy for people in upper-income positions, like Members of Parliament, to be able to say: "Why is it that a family would turn to a local grocery store to obtain the name of a child care service and perhaps check it out in the most rudimentary kind of way?" The evidence is that for most families, certainly for a great many families, it is not a matter of choice; it is a matter of economic necessity. A majority of families find the cost of quality day care prohibitive.
These are just some of the facts, I repeat, that became available to members of all Parties in the House, including members of the Cabinet, who have to assume responsibility for drafting this abomination which they call a child care policy.
I was a Member of the House in 1970 when a Royal Commission reported that the needs for child care required "immediate action". That was in 1970. Today, as the whole country knows, the situation has got worse, not better.
In responding to this worsening situation, in terms of the need, the Government has almost acted perversely. Refusing to see or to respond to reality, the Conservatives cling instead to mythology. They hurl abuse at experts and they are ignoring the modern family in all its diversity.
One of the things that has struck me in observing Conservatives, whether here in Canada or in the country to the south of us, is the amount of lip service that they pay to the family, as if they had some kind of exclusive-and I am tempted to say property-right to the notion of the family. Time after time one hears in Canadian politics and on this continent Conservatives talking about the importance of the family. I want to say, with considerable passion, if they really understand the Canadian family as it exists not in the 1930s but in the 1980s, if there is one group that is ignoring the contemporary family and all of its needs, it is the Conservative Party of Canada. That is the reality.

Hear, hear!
Canada Child Care Act

The Conservatives' so-called National Strategy on Child Care-that is the name that they gave to it-is a strategy right out of George Orwell. It is "double speak" of the worst kind. It is saying one thing, paying lip service to one idea, but moving quite clearly in the opposite direction.
Conservatives clearly have disappointed the people of Canada in many ways since the election of 1984, but there is no greater disappointment in terms of the legitimate claims of the majority of Canadian families than what the Conservatives have offered in this so-called child care policy.
Canadian parents and their children need more rapid access to child care spaces and they need better quality child care. The Conservative Government with this program has delivered neither, but they have taken credit for both.
What is the evidence for what I regard as the severe indictment that I have just made about the Conservative program? I want to point out exactly why I say that. First, the number of spaces without this program has been growing in recent years at the rate of some 15 per cent a year, doubling every five years.
The Conservative promise to add 200,000 non-profit spaces by 1995 might sound impressive on the surface, if one hears just the numbers, until you realize that this actually constitutes a reduction in the rate of growth, from 15 per cent annually to 10 per cent, and instead of requiring only five years to double the number of spaces, with this program that the Conservatives have brought in it will take seven years.
Second, not only have the Conservatives brought in a program which will result in a reduction in the rate of increase in the number of spaces but they have actually put a cap on the growth in these spaces to make sure that by the end of the seven-year program no more spaces will be created than they themselves intended to have created.
Third, there is no requirement in this Bill at all for the provinces, which will be getting federal funds, to offer guarantees that they will actually be providing quality child care spaces as a result of those federal funds.
The conclusion is that the Conservatives have reduced the rate of growth, have put a ceiling on that growth, have ignored quality day care, and then have had the effrontery to describe this as "an effective national child care system". This is a fraud and typical Conservative hypocrisy, that is what it is.
Hear, hear!

When George Orwell was writing his masterpiece 1984, I am tempted to add that he was blissfully unaware at the time that the people of Canada would be electing a government in that very year which would turn out to be the most ardent practitioners of the black art of propaganda that he so vividly described in that master work.

Hear, hear!

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act

We in this Party say that now is the time to embark on a truly national program based on real but varying needs in all of our regions and provinces, and we say that such action would be fully consistent with the kind of federalism that we have decided to renew at the national level of former co-operative federalism that finds itself embedded in the Meech Lake Accord.
Mr. Speaker, the setting of national objectives would be quite compatible with the Meech Lake Accord, but the Government refuses to shoulder its responsibilities. It is not asserting the leadership required to create a Canadian child care program. We can even go so far as to say that there is no program. Although the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) said that their goal is to provide sufficient accessible and affordable quality services, none of this is in the Bill. This Bill attains none of these four objectives.
Let us talk about availability. The normal increase in the number of available places will go down.
Let us talk about cost. There is no national objective and the federal Government has even imposed a budget restriction.
Let us talk about quality and ease of access. Here again there is no national objective. In his speech of August 11, the Prime Minister said, and I quote, "They are the actions of a Government determined to lead in implementing coherent national programs. These actions clearly illustrate that this Government is committed to social justice for all Canadians. Child care is the centrepiece of that commitment." That is what he said!
The Prime Minister has come up with an incoherent program that will create fewer spaces in seven years than will be created by normal growth.
He refused to use the Meech Lake Accord as a tool to develop a Canadian policy for quality child care from coast to coast, a quality program that could very well be implemented by the provincial Governments according to their specific needs. Instead of that, the Prime Minister set no objective. This means that he is overlooking the Meech Lake Agreement. Indeed, he has chosen to ignore this Agreement. That means that the Prime Minister is not showing leadership. On the contrary, he has abandoned his leadership role. He has forgotten Canadian children.

The Conservatives are all so great at talking about the need for choice, as if they had a monopoly on the idea of freedom of choice. Again this has been applied to the program they have brought in. They claim that they will give parents choices by spending $2.4 billion through the tax system.
In the first place, more than half of this money is not new. It was already in the system. In the second place, most of the new money will go to a program which gives parents a maximum of $200 per child per year. As my colleague behind me has said, big deal, and as another child care advocate has said about this sum of money, it will hardly be sufficient to pay for two children's snowsuits. Indeed, if we think of what the Conservatives have done for the average family since they came to power, we can see the kind of shell game they are up to.
Since 1984, the Conservatives have increased taxes on an annual basis. Income and other taxes have been increased by some $1,000 per year for the average family. Here the Conservatives think they will con people into thinking they are doing something effective for children by giving some $200 of that back to parents.
We in this Party say that we should not be playing shell games with the tax system but we should be building an effective and accessible child care system.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my Party is opposing this Conservative scheme because we do believe Canada's children deserve the best and that that should be our goal. We should now be putting in place a comprehensive system of child care. We should be laying down a foundation for such a universal system and we should be doing it now. I regret that the Conservatives have not seized the opportunity to support the modern family in the carrying out of its most fundamental role, the caring and raising of children.
Evidence shows that the first priority of an adequate policy must aim at providing a sufficient amount of money to provide an adequate number of licensed, quality child care spaces that will be universally accessible and affordable for all the families of Canada. Our experience with medicare and public education ought to have been some kind of guide to the Conservatives in drafting this policy.
We would not today have medicare if the Government that first launched that system in Canada, the then NDP Government of Saskatchewan, subsequently followed up on a national basis, had used the tax system and simply gave the money to the people and encouraged them to act as consumers in the market-place and thereby create a universal medicare system. It was simply the failure of the market-place to meet this human need that caused thinking people in Canada and in western Europe to recognize the need for government involvement to create a system that was outside the market. The Conservatives, as is so often the case, learned nothing from history.
As was the case when medicare was first launched, so too now we hear the propaganda from the Conservatives, from the Minister who brought in the Bill and from Conservative spokespersons who write columns in newspapers. They are saying about the New Democratic Party what they said in the early 1960s when we fought to get medicare established. They
August 23, 1988

are saying: "Oh, there they are, those people who want the state to meddle in the affairs of individuals. There they are, they want the heavy hand of the state determining in a day-today way the lives of Canadian citizens, taking away flexibility, taking away variety, imposing uniformity".
These are the cliches we heard in the Conservative opposition to the medicare system in the early 1960s, a system which they now defend. They are repeating those cliches now. They were wrong in the early 1960s about medicare and they are wrong in the 1980s about child care.
The truth is, just as we said that comprehensive medicare in the 1960s would provide freedom for doctors and for patients and particularly freedom from worry about medical bills, so too we are saying about a national child care system that we do not want uniformity. Quite the contrary. I have already said that this measure is compatible with the Meech Lake Accord in terms of its national objectives by acknowledging the differing needs of our different provinces. In that context, some parents in some parts of Canada will want a different kind of child care system for their children, and we want to make sure it is available to them.
We have said that we want diversity, not uniformity. We want a range of options including child care centres, parent cooperatives, after school care, family home child care and neighbourhood drop-ins for parents and children. In short, it is the Tories who are denying flexible, imaginative, variable child care services. It is the New Democrats once again who are arguing for just such diversity to meet the needs of contemporary families.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, I understand that I am about to reach the time limit imposed on me in participating in this debate. I would like to ask for the permission of the House for a few moments to continues.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As is the custom, I am sure the House will agree.
Agreed.

I thank Hon. Members opposite and on this side for their courtesy.
I want to conclude with a positive assertion of the basic elements of what the New Democratic Party is advocating. I have tried to make clear what we find objectionable about the Conservative approach. I want now to say what we would put in its place.
First, we would introduce a Bill that would include an outline of national objectives including a set of principles that would be pertinent to the distribution of federal funds to the provinces with the objective of assuring quality child care. Legislation should require a provincial child care program to conform to the following national objectives: non-profit, comprehensive, quality, affordable and accessible. Each
Canada Child Care Act
province would, within its own domain, pass legislation within this framework setting out its own definitions of these concepts. That would then be assessed according to the national objectives laid down by the Parliament of Canada which would be providing federal funding.
These principles which I have described with respect to the criteria that ought to be spelled out to provinces if they are going to get federal funds are modelled on the Canada Health Act and, as I have already indicated, are fully consistent with the Meech Lake Accord. With these principles in place we would provide the necessary federal leadership but also permit the details of the program delivery to vary to meet the differing needs of families and communities in Newfoundland, Toronto, Moose Jaw and Whitehorse.
Contrary to the assertion of the Conservatives that putting objectives in the legislation would trample on provincial jurisdiction, we assert that this is totally consistent with the model of co-operative federalism that existed in the early 1960s, and totally consistent with the Meech Lake Accord. When we were debating the Meech Lake Accord, if I remember correctly, and I am sure I do, both the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said we could lay down such objectives for a national child care program. They said that when they brought in the Meech Lake legislation. They failed to do it. They ought to have done it.
Second, we would have as a priority the creation of additional child care spaces. We would not only set out a program that would increase the number of spaces in all the variety that I have already alluded to, but make sure they would be quality spaces. Our plan would provide some 50,000 new child care spaces per year on average over the next four years so that we would have 200,000 new non-profit spaces by 1992.
1 want to be explicit about this. In the first year we would be spending S330 million in new money. New spending in 1992 would be as high as $560 million. Including a portion of Canada Assistance Plan spending, which we would keep in place to continue to provide subsidies for low-income parents, we would be spending about $800 million a year in 1992. At the end of the four years there would be about 450,000 child care spaces in Canada at a cumulative cost of approximately $2.3 billion.
During the same period of time the Conservatives would be using up over $1 billion in federal spending additional to what we have advocated, but they would be creating far fewer child care spaces. This is precisely because they prefer to tinker with the tax system and we prefer to get on with the job of providing additional child care spaces.
The third point 1 would like to make is that child care for us has to be affordable. No one is talking about a free system of child care. We do not have free medicare or free elementary schools. We have services that we pay for in our society either

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
in the market-place or as taxpayers through collected tax revenue. What we see as a need right now is a mixture of the two in meeting a real human and family child need in providing affordable child care. By maintaining Canada Assistance Plan subsidies and by maintaining affordability as a national objective, we can ensure a progressive cost structure for child care services.
In the years ahead we believe that paying for child care should be based on the same principles as our progressive tax system. The higher your income is, the greater your capacity to pay, the more you would have to pay. The lower your income is, the less your capacity to pay, the less you would have to pay. Surely we ought to recognize the real need and real and differing capacities to pay for it and get on with the job and make sure it is available.
I want to conclude by referring to what I said at the very outset of my speech this afternoon. The family structure and family life in this magnificent country of ours has changed profoundly in the last three or four decades. From this it follows for us that if we really mean what we say when we say we care for Canada's families and for Canada's children, we have to put in place a child care policy that does not deny this reality but recognizes this reality.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to have the opportunity to ask the Leader of the NDP a few questions about his comments on this very important issue.
He will know, as the Vice-Chairman on the Task Force on Child Care, I had the opportunity of travelling across the country to some 37 cities, along with the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), to deal with the problem of defining child care. In 1970 there was a report dealing with the status of women which laid out all these problems. Yet we found in 1987 and 1988 a remarkable dearth of information about the true nature of the problem.
I know the Hon. Member for Vancouver East must have had some difficulty in her chair when she heard her Leader talk about Orwell and fraud and hyprocrisy of the Conservatives. That certainly was not the spirit of the committee. We had very little difficulty in agreeing on the nature of the problem. Being as respectful as I can, I would accept that there might be different alternatives and solutions. However, I reject categorically the Leader of the NDP's assertion that we are wasting money on tax expenditures. Hundreds of Canadians have been writing me the last two or three months telling me that although the $200 per child is really not enough, and we all know that, try telling them it is nothing when it amounts to $2.3 billion.
I wonder if the Leader of the NDP might answer at least a couple of questions based on this principle. Yes, it is true there are two million Canadians requiring child care. However, 85
per cent of those are currently being looked after in an informal system. A lot of Canadians told us they like that informal system. Some Canadians said they had a great deal of difficulty. Some wanted access to day care and could not find spaces. However, not every single Canadian of that 2 million viewed that situation as a crisis.
Three very quick questions. What does the Leader of the Opposition have to say about his approach to child care, which abandons all those people, fully 85 per cent, who use informal child care and like it? He has not said much today in his speech but in assertions outside he talked a lot about the ideology of the not-for-profit centre. Fully 40 per cent of Canadians in day care, that is the small group that is in formal day care, have their children in the private sector. Would we abandon those in his formula?
The Hon. Member talked about relations with the provinces. Where on earth does he get the information that they can create 50,000 spaces next year? Why do you think you can tell the provinces what to do in an area exclusively under their jurisdiction? It seems to me you are not going to get very far, Mr. Leader of the Opposition, by saying to people like we Conservatives who care as much about the family as you do that our attempt to solve this problem is a fraud. I do not like it and Canadians will not like it, either.

Mr. Speaker, I do want to reply to what I take to be the Member's serious questions. First, I want to be clear, I did not say about the Hon. Member or any other member of his committee that he or they constituted a fraud. I described the Government's policy, brought in by the Cabinet as such, and I took care to say why I thought it was a fraud, and nothing the Hon. Member has just said has deterred me from thinking so. In fact, the Member has confirmed my thinking that what Cabinet brought in was a fraud. If the Hon. Member had understood wrongly what I said about the intentions or the work that was done by members of his committee, I want to tell him I was describing the Government's policy.
There were three specific questions, as I understand, and, by the way, the Hon. Member was asking the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) to answer. I would like to hear what the Leader of the Opposition has to say in this matter also, but as Leader of the New Democratic Party, I will be happy to reply. The first question was what are we offering the family which the Member said was using the informal system, which is very often a euphemism for using a baby-sitter who stays at home. The Member was on the committee and heard a lot of testimony to this effect. The baby-sitter sits before a television set all day long with a small child or small children. Very often that is the situation. I am sure the Hon. Member would not like that anymore than I would. But if the Hon. Member is asking what we are offering to those families, we are not offering anything directly because we want to put it out there
August 23, 1988

so we can have quality child care service outside the home for those who want to have a viable option outside the home.
Like the Hon. Member's Government, we are facing a priority question. Where is the real need? We have listened to the experts, as did the Hon. Member when he was travelling across the country, and we have our experience as parents and Members of Parliament and in talking to people. It is clear that we need new quality spaces made available. That is what we are saying.
Second, I was asked about profit day care. If I understood the legislation correctly, the Government itself finally accepted in its approach for new child care spaces all the best evidence on this, which is that financing will only go for capital grants, starting up a new system should go only to non-profit child care. This is the way we got other social systems under way in this country. The Government itself acknowledges the legitimacy of the point we are making. If we are going to put public expenditures out there for a social service, the general rule should be, and we have applied it here, that it should go for non-profit service for children.
Third, the Member makes reference to the Canadian Constitution and the principles of Canadian federalism. He repeats the Conservative line by asking how we can tell the provinces what to do. I can say very easily that if you, Sir, as a Member of the federal Parliament, were going to allocate federal funds to the provinces for a child care system consistent with what your Leader and your Prime Minister said about the Meech Lake Accord, if you want to set out such a national program with national objectives, flexibly applied according to different provincial needs, then there is a requirement, I say to you, Sir, that the provinces live up to those obligations, that we just do not throw the money out there and pray. We must make sure they live up to their commitments.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I heard the comments about the possibility of giving the provinces instructions. I would like to ask the Leader of the New Democratic Party a question. We all know that Manitoba had an NDP Government from 1982 to 1987. The statistics for this period show that this province had the lowest rate of growth for permits granted to spaces provided by non-profit organizations. This would have benefited the children and families who needed it.

I would like to say that the Manitoba Government during this period had the lowest tax rate for the citizens of this province of Canada and it set a record for job creation-it was second of all Canadian provinces. That is also a fact!
Canada Child Care Act

speechtext: We shall continue the debate now with speeches of at most 10 minutes each. The Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay) has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in a debate on a subject that is of vital importance to our society.
When we look at the day-care situation across the country, we must consider how the situation has evolved in the last ten or fifteen years. When our committee was studying this subject, we found that for 85 per cent of Canadians, day-care is provided in an informal setting. Parents find their own solutions. They often ask relatives or friends to help them or they hire a sitter.
Of course, the Leader of the New Democratic Party doesn't realize that quite often, parents who provide day-care for their children in an informal setting prefer that arrangement because their children feel more secure with one person who takes care of them instead of being in a large group.

We have heard people talk about child care in Canada as a crisis. Well, in some parts of the country it may be a crisis. In other parts of the country it is a problem. In other parts of the country services are available and are being provided. The system of child care without this massive infusion provided for by the federal Government was growing at a rate of nearly 2 per cent a year. People talk about waiting lists as measurements of whether or not there are spaces required in the country. You know how it is with waiting lists, Mr. Speaker, people put their name on one, then another, then another. We found there were Canadians whose names were on 20 waiting lists. There is no doubt that airplanes overbook by 10 per cent or 15 per cent because people put their names on lists.
It seems very clear to me that the word "crisis" is important in child care in some parts of the country, but not everywhere.
In any case, what is more important than whether we define the problem as just a problem or a crisis, is the fact that all we Canadians care more about our children than we care about anything else. We want our children to grow up and be better citizens than we are. We want our country to grow and be better than it is now. Therefore, we are prepared to devote all of our resources as parents and as a Government to ensure that our children receive the proper care they deserve. This is not for me a question of ideology as it is for the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). I do not get up every morning and say: "I am a Conservative. I am for profit centres. They are New Democrats. They are not for profit

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
centres". I care more about the quality of care children receive than I care about who is providing it.
What we have tried to do in this legislation is find a mechanism to respond to all of those things that parents want from their Government.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party has often bragged about the quality of service provided for child care in Manitoba. Let me give him an example. Ideologically, they would not support profit centres. I can document examples in my province of very wealthy parents having their children in subsidized centres while poor parents had to go down the street to the profit centre and pay more. The reason is that not enough spaces are provided. This matter does not deal with ideology, it is a question of doing what is right for young people.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party talked about the relationship with the provinces. My view is consistent with the attitude that in order to work things out in Canada one must work with people. A government cannot sit in its ivory tower in Ottawa and dictate what is good for everybody and decide that every province will do exactly the same thing. The Leader of the NDP gave the examples of medicare and post-secondary education. We have federal legislation in those areas in order to provide funds, but they do not contain minimum national standards in the area of program delivery compared to those he was suggesting. None of the Bills contain such things as doctor-patient ratios or bed-ratios.
Who do we think we are in Ottawa, that we have all the wisdom in the country and that we can tell the provinces what to do because we know better? I will support the right of provinces to make decisions in this area because, very often, the provinces are closer than us to the scene. They know the needs of their own provinces better than we do. Our responsibility as a Canadian Government is to help the provinces and help the parents so that children get the best support we can possibly provide them.
In summary, Canadians care a lot about the children in this country. Even Canadians who do not have children care a lot about the future of this country. It is our responsibility to help the provinces. We are doing that with this legislation.
It is our responsibility to help the parents. We are doing that with this legislation through tax relief. Do not let anyone say, as the Leader of the New Democratic Party said last week in Vancouver, that $2.3 billion in tax relief for Canadians is irrelevant. While it may not be enough, and we would like to do more, we are doing everything we can for the moment. I reject and resent considerably the Member's implication that this policy is a fraud. I think he should go back and read Orwell again. He has obviously missed a few lessons about what it truly means.
This Bill helps Canadians help children. I think it is the greatest piece of legislation we have introduced in this Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate on Bill C-144 which concerns day-care, since the previous speaker said this was the most important piece of legislation tabled in Parliament in the last four years. I would not go that far, but I would say it is a subject that should have received Parliament's attention well before this Government was getting towards the end of its mandate.
Mr. Speaker, I agree that the need for day-care services in this country has become particularly urgent. We know that a tremendous change has taken place in the very structure of the average Canadian family and that in 50 per cent of families with children, both spouses work, so that some form of daycare is necessary, either through day-care centres, home daycare or the help of relatives or friends.
Mr. Speaker, since I am in the same situation myself-we have a seven-year old and a five-year old-I can tell you that for most parents it is a real headache. I am rather disappointed to see that this Bill, which has the full backing of the Government, will do practically nothing about the increasing problems of families where both parents work. Mr. Speaker, today, only 20 per cent of Canadian children have access to day-care and 57 per cent of children between the ages of 6 and 14 are alone after school.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill is supposed to provide about 200,000 spaces, at a time when we would need something like one million spaces. Mr. Speaker, the Government is talking about
200,000	spaces over the next seven years. In other words, it won't do my children any good, although maybe my grandchildren will get something out of it, and all because the Government is nickeling and diming to deal with an urgent problem. The Conservative Government has failed to recognize the changes that are taking place in our society, and the truly pressing need that exists in our cities and in rural areas as well in this country. Take for instance l'Ange Gardien de Rouville, where women fought for this cause and managed to convince the municipal council in a small rural area to set up a day-care centre, and now the demand is increasing. They started with 25 spaces and they think they will get up to 50, and I can tell you this is a success story. But the problem is that this program will not solve the problems that exist across Canada, and the whole undertaking is so fragile, you would think the federal Government tabled Bill C-144 just to pretend it was doing something about the situation.
I advise mothers who are listening to us today and who plan to go back to work in the next six months or the next year not to get their hopes up. Bill C-144 certainly will not solve your problems. Don't count on this legislation to provide day-care spaces. Don't go out and apply for a job right away!
August 23, 1988

Mr. Speaker, usually, once you get the job you make arrangements for day-care. I think the Hon. Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif) is so nervous about the fact that she is probably going to be beaten in a matter of weeks or months that she fails to realize what the situation is. She may have to go out there and get a job herself. But the truth is that one of the reasons why mothers don't go out and look for a job is that they don't have access to day-care. When parents decide, and this is a choice they both have to make, they both want to go to work, what are they going to do with the children? Can they get a sitter? Can they find a space? 1 know. We had the same experience. We applied for spaces in day-care centres, and we had to wait for up to a year or a year and a half for an opening.
This is an urgent problem, and I think the Government is just paying lip service, because it should have introduced measures that are far more energetic than the ones it has tabled.
Mr. Speaker, when I look at the figures, the Government said it wants to help families and it says that families without any taxable income will be entitled to a measly increase of $200 annually in the child tax credit, for each child under six.
Mr. Speaker, you have children too and $200 a year doesn't go very far. I am sure that on $200 a year, if you feed them Similac and buy Pampers, you won't last six months.
I am sure that poor families won't be able to say this program is doing them any good. This is peanuts, when we know how much it costs to raise a family, Mr. Speaker.
And another thing: I think it is clear that this Bill is not very specific about standards and objectives. One wonders exactly what this Government wants to accomplish. One wonders whether it is not just an another example of so-called election goodies. One wonders whether this Government is really serious about what it is doing and if it has any goals, any real family policy that favours a rising birth rate.
Mr. Speaker, the truth is that the Minister is a member of the national impro league, because this is a perfect example of total improvisation. There are no guarantees for universal access. There are no guarantees like ... No other steps have been taken to make it possible for families ... to allow for parental leave or things like that. No consideration was given such measures at all, and no consideration was given to the quality of services that will be available under this program.
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed unfortunate that the Government has failed to do its homework better and really focus on modern family problems in Canada. What can you expect, Mr. Speaker, most Government Members believe that the Canadian family is still structured along the line of the old traditional model. For instance, they do not recognize the reality of single parent families which are among the poorest in Canada and which, under this program, will have no new services made available to them.
Canada Child Care Act
Mr. Speaker, I think that if the tax measures are inadequate, so are the parents' benefits ... They ask for instance for maternity leave to be increased to 26 weeks, parental leave for each of the spouses, top quality services guaranteed, as well as improved accessibility and cost sharing. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, this Bill does not meet the expectations of even the most interested groups.
The great many witnesses who came forward to express their views on this Bill have all criticized its inadequacy and lack of generosity.
Mr. Speaker, we need to think only of the issue of day-care in the workplace. We know that we are taking the very first steps in this direction. There are a few high profile examples, including the Lavalin firm and here in the House of Commons. There are others, but we know that they are unique cases, and the Government should have helped set up daycare centres in the workplace by allowing an over 100 per cent amortization deduction over a five year period to encourage the rapid growth of quality daycare services in the workplace.
Mr. Speaker, you indicate to me that I have only a few minutes left. I am sorry to hear that, because I could tell you about the problems which Canadian families trying to raise children are faced with today, especially the younger ones where both the father and mother went to school and started a career only to find themselves in this predicament... It is not that they do not want to provide their children with the best of care, but none is available. You can visit just about any region in Quebec or the rest of Canada: You better have very good contacts with the day-care centres, or be very affluent; otherwise, you will have to wait years and years for a space. The worst thing is that, generally, it is the wife who has to sacrifice her career and decide to stay home for a year or two while the children are very young. So she suffers a set back in the development of her career. Mr. Speaker, I suggest that
200.000	spaces are just not enough. If you told me that this program would apply only to Quebec, I would say that these
200.000	spaces would make sense.
But since this program will apply to Canada as a whole, Mr. Speaker, we will have to wait seven or eight years. You can imagine that by the time these 200,000 spaces are available, the children who are now 10 years old will be able to exercise their right to vote and be themselves in need for day-care spaces.
Therefore, it is far from beeing enough. I feel also that it is much too late, because this debate should have taken place a long time ago. The Government is trying to pressure us into adopting this Bill quickly. We have only ten minutes at our disposal to express our view on an issue of such tremendous importance for the future of our society.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that Bill C-144 is quite inadequate, that the Liberal Party over the next few months will propose a valide alternative to this Bill, and that we mean to discuss the issue with all the interested Parties, because the Government is showing neither great courage nor leadership on this issue.

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to make just a brief comment on the question that my colleague from across the way raised with regard to my Leader's speech on day care. She tried to portray the record of the Manitoba Government as being a weak record in terms of day care. I suppose she did that in order to try to indicate that the NDP as a federal Government would not have a strong record in this area. Thus she made the statement, as I understood it, that between the years 1982 and 1987 the lowest rate of increase in day care was in the Province of Manitoba.
I am seeking information with regard to this matter. However, in the meantime I want to make note of one thing, that is, if we compare the number of spaces in a province such as Manitoba which has had two NDP Governments, one under Howard Pawley and one under Ed Schreyer, and then compare that with Saskatchewan which has a similar population base, one will see that Manitoba has some 8,771 spaces. Saskatchewan has some 3,698 spaces. There is a Conservative Government in that province, the Government of Mr. Devine. That puts the Manitoba record in a very good light.
The only point I want to make is that we have to look closely at statistics that are being quoted in the House in order to form impressions. I say that because it depends on what statistics one looks at as to what impression one forms. I suggest that it just might be that the Hon. Member across the way selected her statistics in order to put the Manitoba NDP Government in the worst possible light. She did that rather than seeking to provide some objective indication of what the situation is in Manitoba, in which there are far more day care spaces than there are in Saskatchewan which has a Conservative Government.
I have a little more information in this regard. Manitoba has the highest per capita expenditures of all provinces on day care. Why did the Conservative Member not mention that statistic? It reminds me of a book that I read a number of years ago. The title of the book stands out in my mind. It is: How to Lie with Statistics. Rather than using statistics to shed light on a situation, to provide some objective criteria so that we can get a handle on reality, some people use statistics in order to create false impressions, in order to score political points. I am not saying that this is the case here, but one begins to wonder why the Hon. Member quoted one statistic which was the rate of increase statistics rather than pointing out that at the same time Manitoba has the highest per capita expenditures of all provinces on day care.
I wonder if the Hon. Member would have wanted to point out at the same time that there are more spaces per capita in Manitoba, and that Manitoba has the most comprehensive standards in Canada with regard to the quality of care. Not only do we have numbers, a measure of quantity, but there is a measure of quality. Manitoba has the most comprehensive standards with regard to the quality of day care.
As well, I would like to point out that we have increased funding for day care spaces to 11,200 from 6,500. That is a 72 per cent increase from fiscal year 1981-82 to 1986-87. What do you think of that, Mr. Speaker?
