speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate regarding the Government's national strategy on child care. It is one that I am very proud of. I want to focus on the strategies and benefits for Canadian women, and on the impact it will have on women's over-all potential as equal contributors to our country's growth and prosperity.
The national strategy on child care is a very important element of our Government's efforts to help women achieve full equality. It is one of the initiatives that we have undertaken to create an environment that supports and encourages workers of both genders in fulfilling both their employment and family responsibilities.

Our government recognizes that child care is the key to economic equality-that it is a needed and essential social program.
We are committing substantial amounts of money through the strategy to support existing child care services, and to provide incentives for the creation of new quality child care spaces. We have honoured the commitment we made to Canadian men and women to improve the child care system in this country. Moreover, I believe we have done so in a way which respects the choices of parents.
August 23, 1988

In the last twenty years, the social fabric of our society has been profoundly changed as more and more women with children enter the paid workforce and find themselves balancing their combined responsibilities in the workplace and in the home.
In the past two decades we have seen the traditional Canadian family-consisting of a breadwinner father and a mother at home with one or more children-become the exception rather than the rule.
Today 54 per cent of all Canadian women are in the paid labour force. Of women between the ages of 20 and 64, 65 per cent are working outside the home. A full 62 per cent of Canadian mothers with children under 16 are currently in the paid labour force.

An increasing number of Canadian women are raising families on their own. In fact, 83 per cent of single-parent families in Canada today are headed by women.
In some cases, two incomes are needed to keep a family above the poverty line. The National Council on Welfare has estimated that 62 per cent more Canadian families would be poor, if both partners did not work outside the home.
It comes down to the following: Women work for the same reasons that most men work; they work for personal fulfillment, economic fulfillment and, in many cases, out of necessity. The same economic, social, and psychological factors related to employment apply to women as they do to men, and the right to the same choices should also exist for women.
However, women's choices have been constrained in the struggle for equality, whether it is in the workplace, the professions, the business world, at home, or at school; whether they live in rural communities or urban centres. They have been constrained in terms of bringing increased fulfillment to themselves and economic stability to their families by the lack of child care.
It has been a major barrier to women's participation in the labour force. I believe there can be no greater stress on a mother than worrying about the well-being of her child. Not allowing women the opportunity to achieve their full potential means that, as a nation, we are not making the best use of the glorious skills and talents of half our population. That is a situation that we as a society cannot afford, and our future competitiveness and ability to finance ourselves is at stake.
Our child care strategy acknowledges that there is no single solution which can respond completely to the diverse and changing child care needs of Canadian families. For this reason we have offered Canadians a balanced choice of initiatives. The national strategy goes far beyond any child care program ever offered or even contemplated by any government in Canada.
First, the Canada Child Care Act will provide funding to create 200,000 new, quality, subsidized child care spaces
Canada Child Care Act
through new cost sharing arrangements with the provinces. This will go a long way to assure parents not only of the availability of child care, but of care which is professional, safe, and developmentally healthy for their children.
Because we recognize that people are different and want to make different choices, the second part of the strategy consists of two new tax measures which will benefit almost three-quarters of Canadian families with pre-school age children. As a Government we recognize the unfairness of a system that has allowed the bulk of working families incomes to be eaten up by child care expenses. This strategy aims to ease the situation by doubling the child care expense deduction from $2,000 to $4,000 a year for each child under six years of age, and in addition, removing the limit of $8,000 on allowable deductions.
As well, lower income parents and many families without child care receipts will benefit, beginning this year, from the supplement to the child tax credit, amounting to $100 this year, and $200 next year.
In addition, the strategy creates a $100 million child care initiatives fund which will give priority to practical proposals designed to meet child care needs and innovative approaches to providing services.
In total, the Government is committing $6.4 billion to the strategy, including special amounts for native children over the next seven years, and another $1 billion annually after that to support child care in this country.
This strategy goes far beyond anything ever offered. Certainly, for many years the Liberals sat on the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women from 1970 without doing anything about what was looked at then as an urgent problem. The NDP seems to believe that all Canadian families are the same, that all children are the same, and everyone has the same needs.
Crafting our strategy was difficult because the needs of Canadian families are not the same and one solution will not do. A walk down a street in downtown Toronto versus a walk down a street in a small community in Newfoundland, or a drive 40 miles from the nearest community to a farm in Saskatchewan, will tell one that. We heard from people about those problems, and we are determined to resolve them.
The reason that I am happy with this strategy, and the reason that I am very proud of it, is that the fundamental position of the Government is that women have the capacity and the ability to contribute so much to our society. The structures that have existed from the beginning of time where men work outside the home and women work inside the home are changing, and they are changing fast because of economic needs, and because of that great capacity that women have to contribute more fully if they are given the choices. The major constraint on that at the moment is child care, and we are absolutely determined to celebrate those differences that women have, and altering the structures of our society in a way

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
that is positive for them, for their children, and for family life however it may be formed in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to speak on the subject of child care. It is one that I have met on many occasions much more personally than politically. In the raising of our seven children we had many occasions not only to make use of child care, such as was available, but also at times to give child care. A number of my adult children have also done the same.
I agree with the previous speaker that there are many varieties of child care. However, I would also tell the previous speaker that, from my experience as a father and grandfather, the variety that is most needed is non-profit, publicly funded, affordable child care spaces. There will always be other arrangements for those who need them or prefer them, but the great bulk of what is needed is of the type the previous speaker made fun of because it is what the NDP advocates. The problem with Bill C-144, Mr. Speaker, is that rather than building and expanding the child care provision in Canada it limits it. It will provide fewer spaces in six years than would have been provided had the growth of child care places continued as it was under the Canada Assistance Plan.
In 1974, there were 55,181 places. Six years later, in 1980, it had virtually doubled to 109,141 places. In 1986, it doubled again to 220,517 places. Currently, it is up around the level of
243.000	in 1987.
My point is that the Canada Assistance Plan did not set a ceiling, a lid, a limit, and it did not cause the day care providers and managers of the money to set ceilings and limits, all the way down the line. At that rate, by 1994 we would have
480.000	or more places for child care under the Canada Assistance Plan. But the Bill C-144 plan would not allow us to reach that figure until a year later. In other words, it is slowing down the provisions of places for child care. That is bad enough in itself. If it were only that there was to be some shortfall under this Government's plan compared to the plan that we have had previously, but it is worse than that, because the uncertainty created by the nature of this program has caused chaos in at least one major centre of Canada, that is, Toronto, in the provision of child care.
I refer to what was noticed in The Globe and Mail on July 12, in the story entitled "Federal day-care strategy called inadequate". It described the case of a mother who had searched for a year for proper child care for her daughter while she worked. It says:
After weeks on a waiting list, she finally won a space for (her 18-month-old child) in the University Settlement House centre in downtown Toronto.
She then discovered that she could not get a subsidy from Metro Toronto, although she qualified under a means test, because the municipal government has recently resorted to what amounts to a freeze in subsidized spaces.
That is a strange new practice for Metro Toronto social services. It is explained here as follows:
Although it has expanded the number of subsidies, Metro cannot keep up with the demand.
In other words, they are worried about the ceiling being imposed by Bill C-144. The story goes on:
Part of the problem, child-care lobbyists say, is that the federal child-care strategy, which promised 200,000 new subsidized spaces, has given families the impression that the spaces already are available ...
At the same time, the accompanying child-care legislation, widely rumored to be destined for first reading in the House of Commons this week or next, will limit what is now open-ended cost-sharing between Ottawa and the provinces.
Therefore, it explains further down:
The provinces do not want to get caught spending money that may not be matched by Ottawa.
So we have chaos and cut-backs introduced into the whole system by this legislation, even before it is passed. It is simply the news and the confusion of it.
Although that is the worst fault of this legislation, it is not by any means the only one. There is also the serious fault relating to quality, that for the first time federal spending will not be diverted in part to day care centres established for profit.
The Ontario Government has done a study to compare, according to the standards of the Province of Ontario, day care centres run for profit and day care centres not run for profit. On every criterion considered, the profit-oriented day care centres treat the children-not to mention the staff-worse. This confirms what many of us have observed around Metro Toronto, that it is done as a careful study. They point out in a Toronto Star article of May 14, entitled "Non-profit day-care does the best job study shows":
Almost 54 per cent of commercial centres failed to have enough qualified staff as required by the act, compared to 15 per cent of parent- or community-run non-profit centres.
The story also goes on to point out:
Commercial centres took longer than other centres to correct staffing problems. Ninety-five per cent of non-profit centres with parent or community boards solved staff shortages within six months, compared to 77 per cent of commercial centres. In fact, 11 per cent of commercial centres still had a staff shortage after 10 months.
They just do not care as much. If they are running for profit, they will squeeze the money even if they are violating provincial standards.
Given that this Government has refused, contrary to what was implied by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he preached Meech Lake, to put national objectives into the legislation-that is with teeth-it is there in the preamble, perhaps, and in the PR, but not as laws-we can therefore expect provinces to get even slacker than some of them now are, by enforcing their standards.
The story goes on:
Commercial centres more often than non-profit centres had restricted licences because of Act violations.
August 23, 1988

Violations of the Standards Act. Furthermore, commercial centres more often had more spaces than the Act entitled them to have, that is, they were taking children, that they were not authorized to have, much more often than non-profit centres.
My point is that this spending program as proposed by the Government will not get as many day care spaces as we would have under the existing program, and the quality of the care will be worse than it is now. This opens the government funding to commercial outfits, some of whom have demonstrated their complete contempt for any kind of standards of child care, let alone the well-being and good pre-school education of the children.
This law is really a fraud. It pretends to do something that it does not even attempt to do, and if it goes into action it will gravely undermine even what is being done now, to provide day care. If this law is passed, the public, understanding the need of day care for the 60 per cent of families where both parents work, will simply have to throw this Government out and put a Government in that will repeal this law and put in a real child care Act that will meet the need.

I am
pleased to take part in this debate on child care. I would like first to commend my colleague for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) for the quality of the work she has done on this matter on behalf of the Liberal caucus.
Mr. Speaker, under the Governement child care strategy
200.000	spaces are proposed for 1.8 million children aged 0 to 13 years. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, that proposal, that strategy will be implemented over seven years. Can you visualize that,
200.000	spaces over seven years when more than one million are needed now!
There you have the nature of the problem. I heard the suggestion made earlier from Governement benches that they would like to do more but this is all they can afford!
How come then they can afford some $12 billion for nuclear submarines? When it comes to this very important need, they stop at 200,000 spaces. Truly, this is a drop of water in the ocean!
Society has changed dramatically in the past 20 years. Today, less than one in six Canadian families fit the traditional family pattern, the wife at home with the children and the husband out working. Many families are headed by single parents, most of whom are young mothers. And while more than half of all women with pre-school children work outside the home, only about 20 per cent of those children are served by accredited day care centres.
What is more disturbing, only about 2 per cent of every school-age child of working parents, the so-called latchkey
Canada Child Care Act
child, has access to after-school care. Raising children is expensive whether one or both parents work, and providing child care is one of the highest costs.
Inadequate child care is not just a women's issue. It is not just an issue for parents. It is an issue for all of us, parents, employers and governments, every Canadian. 1 believe that all of us have a responsibility, a duty, to be part of the solution.

Mr. Speaker, let us refer to accessibility. Of course, there are people who, under this Government's proposal, can get a tax credit, and a hefty one at that because of their high income and they can afford child care. But what about needy families, those that cannot afford that, especially in my constituency of Saint-Leonard-Anjou, where in the majority of cases, they are single parent families, or families where both husband and wife work because they need the extra salary. Both work because they need the money to maintain their homes, or to pay the rent, or to send the children to school, in order to be part of that new society.
And if we have no strategy, no policy, no Act that can help those families, Mr. Speaker, we will have failed as Members of Parliament. We are not here to help those who are rich, those who have money. We are here indeed to help improve society for people in need. And this Government's legislation, this Tory Government's strategy does not exactly address those problems.
Mr. Speaker, the other problem today is that one only has to walk through our streets, our cities, our towns to realize the number of children, and in a few weeks chidren will be back to school. And how many children will there be? There will be thousands and thousands of "latchkey kids", and that is unacceptable!
Although in our society there is an elementary or high school in every area or district. There is a school! There is a school, Mr. Speaker, and the children go there.
But why can't there be a program, a piece of legislation which would help the provinces to put to use these buildings and facilities which have been paid for by their very taxpayers? Why can't we turn them into day care centres, where children could go during the lunch hour or after school until their parents can come and get them.
Mr. Speaker, that is also a major problem which must be addressed in a child care policy or strategy.
Today, as I was saying, women, whether married or single mothers, don't go to work for pleasure or for sport, they need the money. We must therefore devise policies and laws which help them find quality day care centres for their children while giving them the assurance that their children will be well looked after.
In fact, I think we could look at the school system for a solution. Think about the number of teachers who have been laid off. Before I was elected to this House, I lectured teachers

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
who were retrained and encouraged to switch to a business career, because their jobs had become redundant. Mr. Speaker, why don't we retrain those teachers so that we can provide quality child care services at school? In summer, students are out of school for two months, while most parents only have a two-week holiday. What happens during the balance of six weeks? Couldn't we have summer camps? Mr. Speaker, I speak from experience having taken part in a program put together by a community agency from my constituency, where we were able, for the first time, to use the facilities of four different schools for summer camps. Children living near those schools can go to summer camp and their parents can go to work knowing that their children are being supervised by counsellors.
Mr. Speaker, it is not enough for the government to allow tax credits while letting recipients choose where their children will be cared for while they are at work. It is not enough because some couples have to work to make ends meet and their tax credit is insufficient to solve their problems!
I think that we must first have a policy for all those in need and then reach an agreement with the provinces to create quality child care centres in schools. That would solve a big part of the problem. Finally, the Government must guarantee a certain number of spaces, establish standards of quality and ensure that all Canadian citizens have access to child care services.
You are telling me, Mr. Speaker, that my time is up. There is still the whole issue of flexibility to talk about but I hope I will have other opportunities to do so.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak in support of this bill, the Canada Child Care Act.
The process has been demanding, Mr. Speaker, but we always proceeded with the knowledge that what was going to be presented to Parliament would represent what Canadian parents wanted, and would affect the well-being of children and of family life for decades to come.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the process may have seemed long, for the issues were complex, but it was a deliberate course, thoughtfully examined and re-examined, until the Government was sure that its child care plan was right for children.
Canadians deeply value their children and hold the family unit as a cornerstone of society. Yet, at the same time, Canada is a pluralistic society occupying a vast land filled with diversity of views and needs. The contrasts between rural and urban life, and between different regions of the country, offer up a rich mosaic making Canada unique among nations. It is no wonder that Canadians hold differing views as to how to best meet child care needs.
In respecting these different parent preferences and situations, it was necessary to proceed intentionally and thoughtfully. This was not a task that could be done unilaterally in isolation from families and children. It was a task that required consultation with parents, with deeply concerned citizens, with professional and lay associations, with front line child care workers, and with other levels of government.
We sought a policy which reflected the caring nature of Canadians to which governements would commit their support and resources.
Mr, Speaker, I would like to review with you the process and milestones along the way which resulted in this bill now before the House.
During the summer of 1984, at a debate hosted by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, involving the leaders of the three political Parties, child care emerged as a key issue. As leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, Mr. Mulroney firmly committed his Party to a strong leadership response to address this pressing and urgent issue.
Following the election, this commitment was underscored in the Speech from the Throne, and I quote: "My Government has as a high priority measures to support and strengthen the Canadian family, which is the cornerstone of our society. The need for accessible and affordable child care has in recent years come to the forefront of the social agenda facing Canada. In an effort to reach a national consensus on options in this area, you will be asked to establish a parliamentary task force on the future of child care in Canada."
In proceeding with this commitment it was most important to consult with the Canadian public. To this end, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin), was asked to chair the special committee on child care. The parliamentary task force was established in February of 1986. It was given a broad mandate to go beyond the traditional child care issues and study all aspects of child care. In order to ensure that all Canadians had an opportunity to express their views on this important subject, the task force travelled across the country from coast to coast holding public hearings and receiving submissions.
There was an overwhelming response from individuals and organizations which reflected the importance Canadians attach to their children. While there was great diversity in the views presented to the task force, there were presented many imaginative and innovative ideas.
Between March and June 1986, the special committee on child care heard 1,047 presentations, welcomed 1,632 witnesses, and received 944 written submissions. Canadians who wanted to be heard were heard!
The task force heard from families with special needs. It also heard from native people who felt that culturally appropriate child care services would help them retain their identity and provide an important support to families. Parents of
August 23, 1988

disabled children expressed their concerns about the integration of their children in Canadian society and their own need for support and respite from time to time. Of course, for many members of ethnic minorities, the search for linguistic and culturally sensitive child care services was outlined as a major concern.
Although, as would be expected, the views were remarkably diverse, three common themes were expressed repeatedly: The affordability, availability, and quality of day care.
In October of 1986 child care was reaffirmed by the Government as a high priority in the Speech from the Throne. The Government also indicated, at that time, that discussions with the provinces would begin once the report of the task force had been received.
During this same period of time, Canadians also contacted the Government directly to share their views. Mr. Epp met with a range of national groups, including the Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association.
Through public opinion polls, the federal Government received additional evidence that the views being received by the special committee on child care and through direct contact with citizens, was indeed representative of the views of the country. The polls indicated that while Canadians believed that there were serious problems with the day care system, they were still prepared to assume a considerable degree of the financial responsibility for child care, and wanted the system to offer flexibility.
More than six in ten Canadians indicate a preference for government support for a lot of different day care options and 77 per cent of Canadians with children using day care hold this view.
More than seven in ten Canadians-73 per cent-believe that there are not enough spaces to meet current needs. Parents in general-76.9 per cent-and those parents with children using day care, 78 per cent, are even more likely than average to believe that there are not enough spaces at present.
Almost eight in ten Canadian women, 79 per cent, feel that there are not enough day care spaces available to meet current needs. Women are more likely-76 per cent-to agree that day care is too expensive for the average Canadian. Seventy-two per cent of women believe that the problem of "single parents who are unemployed who could be able to get a job if day care spaces were available for their children", affects a large number of parents.
When asked how governments could best ensure that quality, affordable day care is available to those who need it, the public supported a flexible approach. In this regard, while most believed that the best method was to provide financial assistance directly to day care centres, direct assistance to parents-29 per cent-and employers-30 per cent-also met with support.
Canada Child Care Act
Mr. Speaker, the federal government recognized that in order to have a national child care program, the provinces would have to be collaborators and partners. Much of the child care system does and will continue to come under provincial jurisdiction. Therefore it was essential that the federal Government not only enter into dialogue with Canadian citizens, but that they also consult closely with their governments.
To this end, at the First Minister's Conference held in November of 1986, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) reiterated the federal Government's intention to allocate substantial resources to child care.
During that meeting the Prime Minister also announced that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) would be meeting with provincial Ministers to assist the Government to develop a child care system of the very highest order for Canada. This commitment was honoured in January 1987 when the Minister of National Health and Welfare convened a federal-provincial/territorial meeting of social service Ministers. During that meeting, a target date was established by Minister Epp for confirmation of the federal strategy.
Indeed, most provinces clearly affirmed the federal Government's position that child care, although coming under provincial jurisdiction, was a national issue that would have to be resolved in federal-provincial/territorial partnership.
Of course, the views expressed by different provinces reflected the diversity that exists across the country. However most shared the view expressed by the general public that flexibility, choice, availability, affordability, and quality were essential ingredients to be included in a national program.
In March of 1987 the federal Government received the report of the parliamentary task force on child care, "Sharing the Responsibility". Two minority reports were also received. Having consulted with parents and Canadian citizens; having consulted with the provinces and territories; and now having the recommendations of the task force, the federal Government carefully studied and scrutinized all the data, recommendations, and viewpoints it had received to finalize the federal strategy.
Mr. Speaker, it was an exciting moment, on December 3 of 1987, when the National Strategy on Child Care was announced. A new social program was being offered to Canadians!
The National Strategy offered $3 billion for a new federal-provincial/territtorial program, $2,3 billion for tax initiatives, and $100 million for the Child Care Initiatives Funds.
The next two months were hectic indeed. Government officials travelled to every province and territory to discuss the federal offer in detail and to ascertain preliminary reactions of those who would have the responsibility of implementing the program.

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
Following this round of discussion and consultation with the provinces and territories, a meeting of federal/provincial/terri-torial deputy ministers was convened. During this meeting the provinces were asked to submit their projected expenditure plans and space targets for the next seven years. These plans would provide the federal Government with a firm overview as to the level and degree of provincial and territorial commitment to expansion of the number and quality of affordable child care services in Canada.
Indeed, most provinces responded with enthusiasm and clearly affirmed the information previously obtained by the federal Government, that the child care issue was indeed a high priority for provinces. In fact, the provincial and territorial response went beyond that which was earlier anticipated. The expenditure plans went well beyond the $3 billion announced earlier in December by the federal Government.
This is of course presented an interesting quandary to the Government in that we were delighted that the provinces were responding to our leadership but also very concerned about being fiscally responsible and not committing ourselves to spending more resources than we could afford.
The provincial and territorial plans were carefully studied. The solution reflected the sensitive balance between fiscal responsibility and the desire to make a fully adequate and caring response to the needs of Canadian children and families.
The result was the annoucement this past month that the federal Government was adding an additional $1 billion to the package, $940 million for the enhanced federal-provincial program and $60 million for child care programs for Indians on reserves.
Consequently, we now have before us this Bill which represents an historic milestone in Canadian history. As I have shown, it is a product of broad consultation with interest groups and citizens across the country. Their views and preferences have been subjected to the most careful study and scrutiny, and, I suggest to you, represents a balance of the various perspectives. It involves support to the formal day care sector, to parents using informal child care arrangements, support to the family, extends flexibility to the provinces and territories so they can develop a system best suited for their situation, and it addresses the issues of availability, affordability, and quality.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to raise my voice in support of the Canada Child Care Act, a truly historic milestone for improved child care services in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have an opportunity to take part in this debate on child care. As a former teacher I recognize how important it is that we look after children at an early age. I am sure the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), a former teacher himself,
would agree with me that this is the most important time and it should be a government priority.
One of the things I find despicable is that at the end of four years in government, the Conservatives are just starting to come to grips with something they made an election priority in 1984. They said they were going to move quickly on child care. Yet here we are, one week short of four full years of Conservative Government, and they are only now bringing the Bill forward.
I also find it deplorable that this Bill does not really meet the number one problem facing parents looking for child care spaces, that is, a lack of availability of spaces. Earlier today my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), spoke about what the NDP believes must happen. He criticized the legislation in front of us. In response to his speech, one of the Conservatives got up and tried to indicate that the Province of Manitoba had a poor record under Howard Pawley on child care spaces. I am going to use part of the few minutes I have to set the record straight.
The NDP Government in Manitoba in fact had a very good record of providing spaces and standards for child care. Despite the figures the Government tried to read into the record based on whatever inaccuracies, let us talk about what really happened in Manitoba from 1981 to 1987. Manitoba had the highest per capita expenditure of all provinces on child car, not second, not third, not fourth or fifth, but the highest per capita expenditure on child care. Remember that Manitoba is not a rich province. Remember that Manitoba was also suffering cut-backs in the money it was receiving from the federal Government during that same time. Manitoba did not get the money from the federal Government it was entitled to because of the new formulae originally devised by the Liberal Government under A. J. MacEachen, which was further reduced by the Conservatives when they came into power. Yet Manitoba found the money for that number one priority, our young children.
During that same time period we had the most comprehensive standards with respect to the quality of child care. Again that shows the emphasis that the Pawley New Democratic Government placed on young children in our province. Funding for day care spaces was increased to $11,200 from $6,500, a 72 per cent increase. Some people may say that this is not enough, but over that five or six year period it is a fairly large increase. Obviously more could have been done. Obviously some of us would have liked more to have been done. However, the point is that money was going into that program. The funds earmarked for grants for day care spaces and subsidies to parents increased by 225 per cent during that same time, from $8.5 million in 1981-82, when the Government changed, to $27.5 million. As I said earlier, a 225 per cent increase.
I would like to see the Province of British Columbia match that record. I would like to see the Liberal Government of
August 23, 1988

Ontario match that record, with all the riches it has. I would like to see the Conservative Governments in Saskatchewan and Alberta match that record. Incidentally, the last time I checked, Alberta was not one of the poorest provinces in this country. I would like to see them match the record of the NDP when it was in government. That is why I know, when we look at the speech made by Ed Broadbent in Vancouver last week on child care-
Ed Broadbent?

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Oshawa, the Hon. Leader of the NDP. The most popular leader in the country.
Who? I have told you a million times not to exaggerate.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
They laugh. There are people in this country who are afraid of Mr. Broadbent because he tells the truth. When he was telling the truth on child care, when he talked about the policies and priorities we believe in, the national standards we believe are necessary for child care, people know he means it and that our Party means to bring it about.
It is a comprehensive program because it recognizes the needs of the various provinces. It also recognizes the need for national objectives. That is what is so sadly lacking in the program we have before us today. Despite the fact that the Meech Lake Accord allows the federal Government to call for national objectives when it moves on new programs, the federal Government, on its first important measure after initialling the Meech Lake Accord, failed to set national objectives. I cannot understand why a government that negotiated the Meech Lake Accord would refuse to provide leadership in setting national objectives for so important a program as child care.
We all accept now that medicare had to have national objectives. When we renegotiated the Canada Health Act and introduced legislation on that a few years ago, all Parties in the House agreed there must be national objectives for health care. Why not for child care? To be told that each province is different, that each province has different circumstances and priorities, is not really to answer the problem. We recognize the differences in financing and salaries. We recognize the differences that exist because of regional disparities. However, in my riding we have remote reserves which are setting up child care facilities. If they can live up to provincial standards in Manitoba, obviously the regions of this country can live up to national standards. It is a real shame the Government did not have the political courage to bring those standards into the legislation.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp (Provencher) that Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mrs. Martin (p. 18222).

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few moments tonight to speak to the Government's proposed child care legislation and to offer my Party's response to the same issue. The major social challenge facing Canada today is the urgent need of average Canadians and their families for reliable care for our children. Over 1.8 million children whose parents are in the labour force do not have access to quality child care services. The inadequate number of child care spaces is failing our children and makes it even more difficult for women to participate equally in the workplace. Canadian men and women want government action that responds to the real needs of their families. The Conservative Government of Canada has put forward a charade.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I presume the Hon. Member would like the House to hear the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan. The Hon. Member from Thunder Bay-Atikokan has the floor.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I want to thank my colleague for her intervention drawing the attention of the

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
House to child care. It is a very important issue in Canada today and one that is not being dealt with appropriately by the Conservative Government. This Government's so-called national strategy on child care is an excellent example of Conservative broken promises to Canadian families. After waiting four full years for this Government to keep its promise, or for the Conservative Party to keep the promise of the 1984 campaign to introduce an effective national system of child care, Canadian families have been disappointed once again. Canadian parents and their children need greater access to quality care at lower costs. This Government's scheme will create fewer child care spaces after seven years than would have resulted without it.
The Conservatives have promised to add 200,000 non-profit child care spaces to Canada's existing 240,000 spaces by 1995. That is a growth rate of less than 10 per cent annually. In fact, child care spaces in Canada are already doubling every five years. The average rate of growth over the last four years was 15 per cent.
What is happening under this Conservative smoke and mirrors in child care is that we are actually going to have less child care spaces created throughout Canada-urban Canada, rural Canada, northern Canada, native Canada-than would have been created under the existing Canada Assistance Plan. That is very regrettable. The Government had the opportunity to take a very progressive step to ensure that those families, whether they be mother-led families or father-led families or two-parent families, had the opportunity to have their children looked after in a quality manner by staff who are appropriately trained and appropriately reimbursed for their education and their labours while the parents went out, whether it was one parent or both parents, to work outside the home in order to meet the economic realities of today.
For those of us who come from the larger urban centres of this country, child care is a norm, and there are child care centres in our communities. Some are profit, some are nonprofit, some are municipally run, but there are other communities, particularly in the distant locations, rural locations and the North, where there is no formal child care at all. In the community of Atikokan, one of the communities that I represent in this House, there is not a child care centre or a day care centre; there is only informal care giving through babysitting. While there is every good intention by those care givers, the reality is that most often or not they do not have the skills to provide the kind of quality experience that one can obtain in a municipally operated or a non-profit child care centre that is child focused and family focused.
There is a need to expand the programs. There is a need to ensure that child care is provided not as a means to make profit but as a means to provide services, much needed services to the families of this generation.
I mentioned earlier that the Government's child care program is less than what the current program offers. In fact, it actually puts a ceiling on the amount of child care spaces
that the Government will support. Even worse, the Conservatives are asking the provinces for any commitments as to quality in return for federal funding.
Would you, Mr. Speaker, if you were in private business, give money to a subsidiary company and not ask what it is going to do and not require that it do certain things? Would you, as a banker, give money to a company without having strings attached? Of course not.
What we have been saying and what was provided for in the Meech Lake round of amendments to the Constitution was that national standards be included in the legislation, not standards that would say that you would have to have a child care centre that is 300,000 square feet and employs five staff, but one that would say that if you are going to get federal funds, you must create spaces, you must create new spaces and fund new spaces. We need to develop in rural Canada the kind of spaces that are needed to meet the variations of lifestyle, to reflect the seasonal kind of economy on the farm when children need to be away from the farm so that both parents could work on complicated and dangerous machinery and to keep the young children from underfoot and out of danger. It also applies to a small northern community that has a single industry to function with, to survive with, that operates around the clock, for example, a pulp and paper mill in a community like Terrace Bay where there is need for more than just eight o'clock in the morning until five o'clock in the afternoon kind of child care and a need for overnight services.
There was an opportunity to develop national standards that every province would have to adhere to in order to get federal tax dollars returned to their taxpayers, but they chose not to do that. They chose to be wimpish about it and leave it to the province to say "we cannot interfere". We on this side of the House reject that kind of mentality.
The Conservatives also claim that they are going to give parents choices by spending $2.4 billion through the tax system. In the first place, more than half of this goes to existing tax measures. In the second place, most of that new money will go into a program which gives parents a maximum of $200 per child per year. As a parent I know that in this day and age $200 does not go very far. One child care advocate appearing before the committee reviewing this legislation indicated that a parent would be lucky to buy two snowsuits with that money. If you think about the growth rates of young children, you know that two snowsuits a year is not unheard of. Children grow quickly and put a great deal of wear and tear on their clothes. So this amount is a pittance. The money would have been better used to provide child care spaces in quality and affordable child care centres for the young children of Canada.
There is a better way, Mr. Speaker. I realize my time is running out so I will be brief. We want a program that will meet the real child care needs of Canadians and give Canadian
August 23, 1988

men and women real choices. Priority on child care spaces means a good child care program to establish a base on which we can build good quality child care in Canada, not the ceiling in the government plan. The New Democrat's plan would provide 50,000 new child care spaces per year, on average, resulting in 200,000 new non-profit spaces by 1992. I emphasize non-profit. We would establish a set of national principles in the federal funding legislation which would guarantee quality child care. The legislation should require a provincial child care program and conform to the following national objectives: comprehensive, quality, affordable, accessible, flexible, non-profit, and accountable child care.
These principles are modelled on the principles in the Canada Health Act and are consistent with the Meech Lake Accord. Enhanced maternity and parental benefits are policies which give parents real choices. The Government does nothing about paid parental leave. New Democrats would increase opportunities for parents to stay at home with an infant child by providing enhanced and extended maternity and parental leave benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Finally, we propose 10 days paid family responsibility leave through the Canada Labour Code. These proposals are all designed to spend more time with our children, but when we cannot, it will ensure that children have quality child care available whether they are in Toronto, Thunder Bay, Atiko-kan, or wherever.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to the child care program the Government says it is putting in place. I find it rather sad that from a Government that is supposed to be trying to put a new face on its activities and to keep its promises, we have a Bill that is full of puffery. It is window-dressing and trickery with figures. It will not meet our present needs, and it puts a cap on the natural growth that was already in place.
Under the Canada Assistance Plan, without this new program, the federal Government would have spent, assuming an inflationary factor of only 5 per cent a year, $17 billion over the next seven years. The total federal spending over that same period of time could now be slightly more than $22 billion or 4 per cent per year more than we now have without this new program.
On top of all that, there is a catch. We do not know if even one nickel will be spent in each of the provinces. It takes a federal-provincial agreement with each province to put this into place. As Marjorie Nichols points out, we have to use a conditional tense when talking about child care anywhere within Canada. Certainly we will not have a national child care system with national standards and objectives which must be met.
We talk about the low birth rate in Canada. We talk about our concern for the family and the family structure. We talk about children as being our future. One of the most important building blocks in our society is the child care system, whether it is for pre-school children or for school children with two working parents, children called latchkey children.
I become dreadfully sad when I recall going before the royal commission on the status of women, chaired by Senator Florence Bird. We brought the concern over latch key children into the public view, and we discussed how important it was to ensure that these children had good supervision after school hours so that their parents could work with free minds. Their parents needed two salaries to make ends meet. At that time, we were talking about the working poor but now we are talking about all families. The traditional family with the mother staying home is only one out of every ten families. We are not facing the reality of the society in which we live.
We will not end up with a national program; we will end up with 10 separate agreements with 10 different standards. According to the Meech Lake Accord, we were supposed to have national objectives. This new look at the Constitution would provide for good cost-shared programs with the thought that across Canada there would be equivalent programs. There is no dazzling multi-billion program for day care across this land.
The spending increases will be absolutely minimal. In fact, they are paltry, to use the word of Marjorie Nichols. About $570,000 a year would be made available beyond what is already available under the Canada Assistance Plan. Further, the provinces that want to enter into the national day care
August 23, 1988

program have to opt out of the Canada Assistance Plan. A cap has been put on the growth of this very key sector in society.
I believe that when Conservatives are out on the hustings and have to face the electorate, they will be very embarrassed by the fact that no one will be tricked into thinking that saying that they have put in a great national child care system means that they have really done so, because they have not. In reality, this let's pretend child care program is supposed to provide $6.4 billion over seven years, but $2.3 billion of that total is in the form of new tax deductions on credits announced in the February Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). I am not against that, but those are certainly not new dollars for new child care spaces.
The child care legislation we are addressing today contains exactly $4 billion. However, we have forgotten that $1.9 billion of that $4 billion is already being spent annually by the federal Government through the Canada Assistance Plan on child care items. We have in reality a provision for $2.6 billion in new federal funds for direct spending, from which the $1.9 billion that is already being spent annually is subtracted, ending up with that marvellous amount of $560,000 a year being made available for new programs. That new money will certainly be sufficient for the much needed 200,000 spaces, but that will not answer the needs of another one million children who need this service.
Our Party feels that parents should have the right to choose, but they should also have the right to choose child care services that will be of quality, that will be affordable, and that will have standards for the teachers who will be paid commensurately as they provide the loving care that is needed for young children, and they should have programs in which they will have a say. None of those things have been articulated in this Bill, and I regret the sleight of hand, the use of language which is not reflected in reality in this Bill.
The unvarnished facts are embarrassing to the Government. I hope that each and every government Member will feel the discomfort as their constituents ask them about this not-national, not-good, poorly-conceived child care plan which they think will help the development of Canada and its future. I would suggest that when this Bill goes into legislative committee, government Members carefully consider the kinds of amendments that will truly reflect the needs of our children and their futures in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate having the opportunity to say a few words on the child care Bill, Bill C-144. I will take my allotted time to speak particularly about rural Canada.
This time of year in rural Canada should be time of rejoicing and abundance while in the process of harvesting the crops. Right now, however, the farm community is not a happy community, and there are good reasons for this.
For the last five or six years, the impact of the economy has been building up to the point where farm communities are in a
Canada Child Care Act
very bad state. Prices have risen considerably in the last little while, but that is not having the impact it should on the farm community.
Rural Canada is made up of something over 200,000 farms and the villages and towns with their schools, churches, and medical facilities which serve those farms. For the last several years an average of eight farmers per day have been leaving the farm for reasons such as bankruptcy, foreclosure, and so on. That has not slowed down. In fact, the number is increasing each year. Consequently, farming communities are becoming more isolated. It is because of this situation that farming has become one of the most stressful occupations in the country. The farm suicide rate has tripled since 1981 and now stands at double the national average. There are many cases of rural family violence, much more than we ever thought would happen on the farm.
The bulk of farmers having financial problems are those between the ages of 30 and 45 years. They are highly productive farmers who have committed themselves to farming and they produce a great deal, but they are unable to keep up. It is those same families who have young children that need care.
Those farmers who are staying on the farm and those people in the small communities surrounding the farms are the people we are concerned about right now. A lot of the people leaving their farms are just moving into the surrounding towns or the nearest city. However, a lot of them are attempting to hang on, and they are the ones we need to talk about specifically.
There are probably three categories that we can point to of people who are attempting to stay on the farm and need some assistance with child care. There is the family where one or two members go to the nearest town or city to work. At the same time they attempt to keep the farm going.
There are farm families who move to the city so that the man, in most cases, can drive out to the farm and keep it going. There is a third group which has to be recognized as well. This group stays on the farm but attempts to eliminate all outside help. They try to keep the farm going with the family alone. Every member of the family has to take some responsibility for keeping the farm going.
Right now some farm men and women, in fact perhaps more women than men, are actually doing three jobs at the same time. They are working at a store or office in town, teaching school or driving a school bus to bring in some cash. They also take a certain amount of responsibility to keep the farm going. They do regular farm work and assist in keeping it going. They also take care of the children, raise the family.
Right now child care is a very unpopular concept in rural Canada because there is nothing in this Bill that indicates that rural Canada will be taken care of. There is nothing to indicate that they will have child care in those areas. As one lady told me yesterday, this is another federal program which we in

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
rural Canada will not be able to access. In most cases this involves small towns and villages of 50 to 75 people.
That is one of the things wrong with this approach to child care. We need to look at the specific requirements of rural Canada and make sure that either child care spaces or other arrangements can be made to make sure that the family is able to stay together and keep the farm going.
The federal Government spends huge amounts of money on things which are far less important to Canada than the raising of a family. We should not hesitate to pay people to assist the parents in raising their children. Doing that is a good investment for Canada. We should do it in such a way that it reaches out to those areas and those people who need it most.
Right now many people in rural Canada need assistance in raising their families. They need child care. Consequently, we should provide the spaces or provide the people or the money so that they are able to do a good job of raising a family. This Bill does not indicate to the rural community that any real care has been taken with respect to child care in rural Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate on this legislation, the Canada Child Care Act. I believe it is an initiative which will enable our Government to implement a major part of our new national child care strategy, which includes not only the provisions of this Act but the creation of 200,000 additional child care spaces. As well, there is the tax assistance to families which will be of great benefit to many men and women across this country, and the child initiatives fund.
It is interesting to look at the whole issue of child care and who should be responsible. I am pleased to see a change in attitude across the country on this issue. Recently the Vancouver Board of Trade, the largest business organization in Vancouver, issued a copy of its report making a case for quality child care services in British Columbia. It notes in its report that by the year 2000, 80 per cent of all new workforce members will be women, minorities, or immigrants, and that one-half of all women employees will have babies while they are employed. These facts translate into a need for employers of all types and sizes to deal with child care issues for their own self-interest. In fact, the Board of Trade quotes from some studies done by Fortune Magazine which report that 41 per cent of parents surveyed lost at least one day's work in the three months prior to the poll in order to care for sick children, and nearly 10 per cent took three to five days off for such purposes. Child care problems were also a major cause of unproductive time at work or the production of lower than normal quality work. Obviously, by addressing the child care issue, businesses can achieve greater stability and productivity in their workforces.
It is very interesting to note that the Vancouver Board of Trade goes on in its brief to suggest certain initiatives that the
provincial Government should take to respond to our new federal child care strategy and it went on to outline what it believes employers should be doing. The whole issue of child care is a relationship of four parts: the family, the parents, the employer, and the federal and provincial Governments. Each has a role to play in order for us to address the situation.
I am pleased that the legislation before us provides for the implementation of the goal which was announced last December, "an additional 200,000 new subsidized spaces which will require a federal commitment of some $3 billion". However, on the basis of the plans submitted by the provincial Governments over the last six months, it has become clear that additional financial assistance would be required if we were to meet the goal of 200,000 spaces, as well as ensure the quality of the system as a whole and that the existing spaces continue to improve.
We are aware that just last month the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) announced on behalf of the Government that we were committing an additional $1 billion to the child care program. We are not prepared to sacrifice quality for quantity. Both are equally important to parents whose children will be utilizing the child care system.
Just to share some information about how this new system will work, during the next seven years, which we are calling the "boost period", we intend to support the creation of 200,000 additional subsidized child care spaces. In effect, this will double the size of the current subsidized system. It has taken about 15 years for us to reach the level of 200,000 spaces and in seven years we will double that.
To assist the provinces, because delivery of the services is a provincial responsibility, we will provide 75 per cent of the capital costs involved in the development of new spaces in nonprofit child care agencies during the seven year period. As well, we will provide for 50 per cent of ongoing operating costs for both non-profit and commercial agencies. There have been a lot of questions of why "both", and certain groups have said only non-profit agencies should be eligible for the subsidies. However, we made the decision to include commercial agencies under the terms of the legislation. We recognize that we cannot ignore the basic fact that a full 40 per cent of subsidized child care spaces now being provided are being provided by the commercial sector. The reason our national policy on child care is a workable policy is that it builds upon a system that currently exists and adapts to the regional diversity of this country.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, from my involvement with child care, there is obviously some agencies that are better than others, but I have found excellent child care facilities operating in the commercial sector and excellent facilities working in the non-profit area. I do not believe that either side should be penalized, and I am pleased to see we have included both in our strategy.
This legislation will also permit the Government to increase the rate of cost sharing for certain provinces based upon a
August 23, 1988

national average entitlement per child formula. We have included this special provision to assist parents and children who reside in provinces which are attempting to catch up to other parts of Canada in what they spend on child care. This is a national strategy. We believe that child care facilities and services should be more available in all parts of the country.
1 might point out that Clause 4 of the legislation sets out the various terms and conditions which will form part of a negotiated agreement between the federal Government and each province. These will include the annual federal commitment to the province, the number of spaces to be created during the seven-year period, and the basis for subsequent cost sharing agreements with respect to child care services.
I wanted to respond as well to some comments made earlier by the Eton. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) who indicated that the current provisions under the Canada Assistance Plan would have resulted in $3 billion a year being spent on child care services. She is wrong. That is not the reality. The reality is that at the moment, between the federal and provincial Governments, we are spending about $480 million of which $160 million is federal money. Therefore, the provinces are spending $320 million a year. There is no way the provinces are going to be able to increase their expenditures, so they could theoretically take advantage of the maximum CAP funding. That is just not the real world.
In fact, the present CAP provisions do not include funding for the capital cost for the building or renovating, so there is no assistance there. There is no incentive for the creation of new spaces. Even in the operating area where it is 50 per cent of eligible costs, there are many costs which are not eligible. What actually occurs is that the federal Government ends up subsidizing only about 35 per cent of the total costs. The changes in the new child care strategy in the legislation we have before us, as I mentioned, are 75 per cent on capital cost and 50 per cent on operating and new criteria for establishing that 50 per cent. In the first year alone our contribution will double, and by the end of the seven years it is estimated that the federal contribution will be in the order of $800 million a year.
We will have spent, then, the estimated $4 billion for the creation of those spaces. This legislation is important to the women, to the parents, and to the children of this country. I would ask my colleagues on all sides of the House to give it early consideration so that the system can go into effect, the provinces can complete their negotiations, and those who are involved in establishing a child care agency and child care spaces can get on with the job of creating the spaces and the opportunities for families to have child care available to them.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to participate in this debate. I would like to preface my comments by thanking my Liberal colleagues who have allowed me to speak first so I can go home and spend some time with my daughter. We talk about Parliament and the opportunities for women being equal with men, but the reality
Canada Child Care Act
is that when we are having sitting sessions until ten o'clock every night, week upon week, to try to shove some government Bills through, that is simply not happening. That is just a practical note, Mr. Speaker.
I would also like to spend some time outlining what I consider the giant fraud being perpetrated on the people of Canada in the over-all area of child policy. Let us not forget that this so-called child care policy is coming from a Government that has done everything in its power to cut back the purchasing power of the ordinary family. It has cut back on the child tax deductions from about $370 to about $60 over the course of its time in office. It has cut back on family allowances. What we should really be seeing here tonight is an overall policy for children which really does permit parents to make real choices.
Government Members tried to deindex senior citizens' pensions and they were not successful, but they were successful in doing it with the family allowances because families with children are not necessarily the most powerful voices in our society.
I only have 10 minutes so I would like to focus on what I consider to be the glaring contradictions in this so-called national policy for children. When parents are put in a position, either by choice or by economic necessity, of working outside the home and having to put their child in care other than their own, they want to be sure their child is safe.
I think that is the paramount concern of every parent. That is why the Government must include some national standards in announcing a policy. Yet, it has failed miserably in doing so because the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) is introducing a Bill that permits the provinces to set whatever standards they want. There is no national level of care whereby parents in Corner Brook, Newfoundland, should have the same level of care for their child as a child in Toronto. That is not the case because there are no national standards.
According to the preamble of the Bill, the Government caps the amount of spending. Rather than indicate that the program will expand, it is putting a lid on it.
The previous Liberal Government established a program of subsidized child care spaces that was geared toward low-income earners. There was no limit on that program. The Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) was wrong when she said that the only difference between the previous Liberal program, which was instituted at a time when we were not even sure about the so-called child care crisis, was spending an amount of about 4 per cent per year.
There are no national standards in the Tory child care plan. There are rather generous tax deductions. The tax deductions are being doubled from $2,000 to $4,000 a year per child. As a parent who is earning a salary that is significantly above the

August 23, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
national average, I stand to benefit much more directly from the Government's child tax deduction than a woman in my riding who is working at the Hamilton General Hospital and may be earning $6 an hour.
If I am in the 50 per cent tax bracket and I get a $4,000 tax deduction, that is money in my pocket. However, a woman who is earning $6 an hour and is paying only 15 per cent or 20 per cent in income tax, her benefit is cut by two-thirds. We believe that the tax deduction system is wrong and should be replaced by a tax credit system which would see direct payments to parents, but would start by giving the most money to those parents who are at the lowest end of the income scale.
When one considers the lack of national standards and the fact that the child tax deduction will benefit the rich, it provides a rather clear picture of what policy the Tories want to establish. It has no national objectives.
What have we seen from the New Democratic Party? Its Leader announced that he would like to cut child care spending by about 30 per cent. He wants to spend about 30 per cent less than the Conservative Government, and will do that by eliminating any direct payments to families. A steelworker in my riding who gets a $2,000 tax deduction would lose that under an NDP Government.
Under an NDP Government, the Liberal initiative of a tax credit which would be more beneficial to the low and middle income earners would also be gone. The NDP does not believe in the right of the individual to make choices for themselves. It believes that everything should be run by the Government in an institutionalized fashion.
Wrong, and you know it.

Let me speak from personal experience. I have a terrific child care giver in my neighbourhood in Ottawa. Her name is Clotilde Keklikian. She has just given birth to another child of her own and now has three children. I probably could not have found a better care giver than her under any circumstances. She happens to have voluntarily associated herself with a licensing service. She would meet the need for national standards, but because she receives payment in her home, according to the NDP definition she is part of the massive profit-making conspiracy that would, of necessity, not be allowed under their policy.
Is that making a profit?

I am very happy to hear the NDP defend its policy because I am rather shocked that it would introduce a situation in which a woman like Clotilde Keklikian would not be able to qualify under its system.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member knows full well that the NDP supports family home day care. The woman to whom she is referring sounds like an excellent care giver. There is no reason why she should not be licensed. In fact, she would have many advantages with
extra subsidies under our plan if she were licensed as a family day care giver.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the Hon. Member for Vancouver East will make a few comments on this matter later tonight. The Hon. Member for Hamilton East has the floor.

The NDP has not answered the basic question. Why is it cutting $3 billion from a child care program? There are parents who are currently spending thousands of dollars. Certainly it is very difficult for a steelworker in my riding to come up with the money that is necessary, yet under an NDP Government, that steelworker would probably see a reduction in his disposable income by some $1,000 to $3,000, depending on the number of children. The NDP is wiping out any direct tax credits or tax deductions to families. If that is the case, I would like the NDP to explain why its Leader said last week that he would be spending about one-third less of what is being spent under the Government's program.
There are some fundamental differences. The Liberal Party wants national standards. We also want tax credits as opposed to tax deductions. I have not heard the NDP speak out on this. According to the NDP definition, those who are in family care, who meet national standards and may be making a small profit, would be out of the picture. We believe that those people can also give good care.
Most important, the Liberal Party would introduce a child policy that supports all families and that offers women real opportunity and real choice, not simply a government program, which, over seven years, will result in a near 4 per cent annual increase in spending.
We want to see a program directed not only toward women and families who are working outside the home, but also toward women working in the home because we believe their contribution is just as valuable.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof.
I think we can conclude after what has been said so far, Mr. Speaker, that all three Parties agree on the substance of this Bill. We all agree that today, day-care is becoming an increasingly essential service. However, we do not agree on how funding should be allocated and made available to the public.
Mr. Speaker, I think that first of all, and this is very important, it is a matter of philosophy. I heard my colleague speak earlier about deductions and tax credits. We have opted for tax measures. Other political parties, groups and individuals who made their positions known across this country told us we should focus on establishing a national service paid for by
August 23, 1988

the State, to ensure the availability of such services and provide a number of guarantees. That is more or less the position taken by the NDP. However, in the first place, it is a matter of philosophy, a matter of how we look at the services to be offered to the customer and how we react to an increasingly pressing need.
Mr. Speaker, we can either provide the money or provide the opportunity to spend that money. We have opted for the former.
1 remember, and I think we have lived long enough with a Liberal Government to understand the Liberal approach, when we had an economic problem. The Government invented the Canada Works projects, so-called winter works, in the belief that by creating temporary jobs, it would be able to deal with economic problems, and so billions of dollars were spent every year. The Government spent enormous amounts of money on Canada Works projects which tended to come back every year, with a few new ones. That was one way of looking at the problem.
The Conservative Government and its Prime Minister, Brian Mulroney, decided to opt for another solution, more in line with the philosophy of the Conservative Party, which is a philosophy of free enterprise, a philosophy of supporting developers. It provides Canadian decision makers with the economic conditions that tend to attract investors. That is the big difference. Our opponents however, would set up a program and then they would decide to index it. .. all of a sudden they discovered indexation. That was a wonderful discovery. After sliced bread, indexation is just about the best thing ever invented in Canada. Indexing means that starting today, tomorrow will be like yesterday, but indexed, a little better than yesterday. We cannot build an economy that way! I have never bought clothes from a tailor by saying that I would pay last year's price, indexed. I never bought a car that way, but we have built an economy that way. My colleague was just talking about it. He talked about family allowance, old age security pensions, the MPs' pension fund. It covers everything!
But in my opinion, it is not the right way to develop the economy because it does not teach individuals how to fish-it gives them fish. If in one year they needed a certain amount and the next year the economy has grown by 3 per cent, automatically they are given a 3 per cent increase-that is indexation. We, for our part, give people the opportunity to choose. And in doing so, Mr. Speaker-our program was so popular, we wanted to add about 200,000 spaces and we will have to give out money; we have to give out more money because of the very positive response from the provinces.
We must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that child care is a provincial responsibility. And so on . . . We could not stick our nose in a field of provincial jurisdiction even if we wanted to. We can set up a national program that the provinces could join, that the federal Government could participate in and that would gradually bring people up to the national standards.
Canada Child Care Act
The Liberals suggest directly administering a program in a field of provincial jurisdiction. They are telling the provinces that they are incapable of running day care facilities, just as they are unable to read the Free Trade Agreement, so the Liberals would do all that for them. They tell the provinces not to worry, that they will decide for them and run the day care centres, even if it is a provincial responsibility, and they will force the provinces to accept national standards.
We too, Mr. Speaker, would like to have national standards of quality, and they are being developed, but this necessarily involves each of the ten Canadian provinces and each of the territories. This means that we will end up one day with quality standards that already exist in many provinces, but we will reach them at different rates. That is another foundation of the policy put forward by the Party, that we respect the rate at which each province progresses.
It is clear that Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland have different rates of growth for a social product or program. One only has to look at a province's wealth and existing services, how developed its education services are, what work opportunities there are. Because of all that, the rate and support. . . support at that rate will start for a national program, and that is important for federal programs. All the policies we put forward, that sometimes lay in a grey area between federal and provincial jurisdictions, always led us to respect provincial rates of action, and this is what makes this Government different.
In my first year here, Mr. Speaker, I was Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Hon. Flora MacDonald, with whom I worked more closely at that time. We opened negotiations with the Province of Quebec, among others, on training programs. You are fully aware training programs are a long-standing contending issue between federal and provincial Governments, training being a provincial matter.
